Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines

Computing methodologies RenderingCCS: Computing methodologies Reflectance modelingCCS: Computing methodologies Dimensionality reduction and manifold learningCCS: Computing methodologies Neural networksCCS: TOGJournal: 45Volume: 625712DOI: 10.1145/3842506Jiaqi Yu email: jiaqiyu0307@outlook.com, , Affiliation: University of YorkYorkUnited Kingdom, Dar’ya Guarnera email: darya.guarnera@york.ac.uk, , Affiliation: University of YorkYorkUnited Kingdom and Giuseppe Claudio Guarnera email: claudio.guarnera@york.ac.uk, , Affiliation: University of YorkYorkUnited Kingdom, , Affiliation: Lumirithmic LtdLondonUnited Kingdom2026

Abstract.

Spectral rendering reproduces the wavelength-dependent appearance that RGB rendering cannot: metamerism, colour shifts under spectrally rich illumination, coloured glass, metallic reflection and subsurface scattering. It requires a spectrally aware renderer, but the rendering ecosystem is predominantly RGB: game engines, cloud render farms, GPU rasterisers and most offline renderers consume RGB alone, with no access to the internal wavelength propagation that spectral rendering relies on.

We introduce , a compact linear representation that enables general spectral rendering through RGB pipelines. A trained encoder compresses any visible-range spectral quantity into a small latent vector; the codes are packed as RGB triplets and processed by an off-the-shelf RGB renderer. The codec preserves the arithmetic of light transport, exactly for scaling and addition and approximately for element-wise products, so two standard RGB passes suffice to produce results closely matching a full spectral rendering. The same codec handles reflectance, illumination, coloured glass, conductors, and participating media: one pipeline across material classes, with no per-material modification to the renderer.learned spectral codesunmodified

Where spectral asset data is unavailable, lightweight neural upsamplers bridge legacy RGB inputs to the latent space. Across diverse materials and illumination, the method yields substantial quality improvements on the cases where RGB rendering fails most visibly, at rendering cost comparable to efficient spectral-sampling techniques and with no changes to the renderer.

spectral rendering, spectral compression, RGB rendering pipelines, multi-pass rendering, spectral upsampling, Hadamard product, metamerism

Keywords:

†by†cc-license:

1.

Spectral rendering propagates full spectral distributions through the rendering pipeline, reproducing wavelength-dependent phenomena that RGB rendering cannot: metamerism, prismatic dispersion, and thin-film interference . Modern spectral renderers achieve this efficiently: hero wavelength sampling  and GPU-accelerated spectral path tracers  bring spectral rendering to near-RGB cost in open-source and custom production pipelines.()Watanabe et al., 2013()Wilkie et al., 2014()Murray et al., 2021

Much of the wider rendering ecosystem, however, remains RGB-based. Spectral pipelines such as Manuka  exist in production, but commercial game engines, open-source suites such as Blender, GPU rasterisers, cloud render farms, and most proprietary offline renderers expose RGB inputs and RGB framebuffers only; modifying them to propagate stochastic wavelengths is impractical.()Fascione et al., 2018

Recent work delivers individual spectral effects without touching the renderer core: Tominaga et al.  render fluorescence through Mitsuba 0.6’s spectral build by encoding the re-radiation into per-channel inputs, and Fichet et al.  obtain a similar effect with a reduced re-radiation matrix implemented at the shader level. Fluorescence itself lies outside our supported regime, so these methods are complementary to ours.()2026()2024

Rendering general spectral content through multiple passes of an RGB pipeline originates with Darling et al. , who relight scenes with a fixed six-channel parametric basis. We generalise this assets-only route, which requires no custom code anywhere: a single representation for per-channel-preserving spectral transport across reflectance, illumination, glass, conductors, and participating media, rendered through entirely unmodified RGB renderers. This representation, a , is a compact latent vector $z\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ that supports the per-channel arithmetic an RGB renderer already performs: scaling, addition, and element-wise multiplication. Spectral quantities encode into $z$ ; the codes pack into $k/3$ RGB triplets; the renderer processes them in $k/3$ unmodified passes; a final decode recovers the spectral radiance (Fig.  illustrates the full pipeline). Whether the renderer is Mitsuba, Blender Cycles, Maya Arnold, KeyShot, or a real-time rasteriser (Unreal Engine 5) is immaterial: each processes RGB triplets per channel, which is what the codec requires.()2011learned spectral code2

Exact preservation of all three operations is impossible whenever the code dimension $k$ is smaller than the number $n$ of spectral bins (Sec. ), so the encoder is approximate by necessity. Our linear, non-negative architecture preserves scaling and addition and is trained to approximate element-wise multiplication on the manifold of natural visible spectra. Since each RGB pass carries three channels, practical operating points are multiples of three; Sec.  establishes $k{=}6$ as the smallest configuration that is meaningfully more accurate than a standard RGB pipeline, with $k{=}3$ blocked by a Luther–Hadamard trade-off (alignment with the colour-matching subspace  against Hadamard preservation) and $k{=}9$ unwarranted in quality terms.3.2exactly6.1(; )Ives, 1915Luther, 1927

The codec is content-agnostic: the same encoder–decoder embeds reflectance, illumination, transmittance, conductor IOR, and absorption and scattering coefficients into the same latent space (Sec. ); two per-pixel upsamplers project legacy RGB assets onto the codec’s manifold (Sec. ). Our scope covers wavelength-preserving interactions; wavelength-shifting effects (fluorescence, dispersion) lie outside the supported regime (Sec. ).457

Contributions.

  • (1)

    A , jointly optimised so that iterated per-channel products of the resulting $k$ -dimensional codes remain accurate. This codec compresses any visible-range spectral quantity and enables general spectral rendering through unmodified RGB renderers in $k/3$ standard passes (Sec. ).learned non-negative spectral basis and its dual4

  • (2)

    for legacy RGB assets that target the codec’s $k$ -dimensional manifold rather than full $n$ -channel spectra (Sec. ).Latent upsamplers5

  • (3)

    A establishing $k{=}6$ as the practical operating point: $k{=}3$ blocked by a Luther–Hadamard trade-off, $k{=}9$ unwarranted in quality terms, and the learned basis irreplaceable at $k{=}6$ (Sec. ).capacity analysis6.1

    • We evaluate the codec on broadband, narrowband, and multi-peaked illumination across surface reflectance, coloured-glass transmission, conductor reflection, and homogeneous and heterogeneous subsurface scattering; the teaser (Fig. ) exercises all of these in one scene. We benchmark timing and reconstruction quality against Mitsuba 3’s hero wavelength sampling at matched resolution and spp, and we deploy the codec across four production renderers (Sec. ).16

    2.

    2.1.

    Most compact spectral representations, ours included, are linear decompositions. Peercy  introduced low-dimensional point-sampled representations for spectral rendering; PCA has been applied to reflectance and illumination datasets  and to measured material capture . PCA admits negative entries; NMF  is non-negative but needs more dimensions. Both serve as baselines in Sec. .()1993()Otsu et al., 2018(; )Matusik, 2003Guarnera et al., 2017()Berry et al., 20076.1

    Parametric representations replace the data-fitted basis with a constrained family. Peters et al.  encode bounded spectra as Fourier moments with a maximum-entropy reconstruction, achieving 3–8 coefficients with smooth, energy-conserving output. Karimipour et al.  represent reflectance as $3\!\times\!3$ matrices fitted to cone responses, reaching $\Delta E_{94}\!<\!1$ under broadband illumination but degrading to $\Delta E_{94}$ up to 16 under narrowband sources. Both compress accurately but provide no algebra on the compressed codes: the product of two compressed spectra cannot be evaluated without decompressing first.()2019()2023individual spectra

    2.2.

    Hero wavelength sampling  carries one stochastically chosen wavelength per ray with several stratified companions, reducing colour noise at near-RGB cost. West et al.  generalise wavelength importance sampling to a continuous multiple importance sampling framework, and van de Ruit and Eisemann  build coarse screen-space estimates over multiple passes to guide subsequent sampling. These methods improve efficiency a spectral renderer; we target renderers with no spectral path at all.()Wilkie et al., 2014()2020()2021within

    2.3.

    Converting RGB textures to plausible spectra is a long-standing problem. Smits  introduced a scaled basis-spectrum conversion with a long production history: the Manuka renderer relied on a Smits-style optimisation for all its uplifting , and recent versions replace it with the moment-based method of Peters et al.  for reflectances . Meng et al.  introduced a physically meaningful uplift over the XYZ space. Jakob and Hanika  parameterise the sRGB gamut with three coefficients, smooth and energy-conserving; the method is now standard in PBRT-v4  and Mitsuba 3 . Jung et al.  uplift gamuts wider than sRGB by adding fluorescent components. Belcour et al.  give metameric one-to-many uplift for textured assets. Tódová et al.  constrain the uplift so that selected spectra are reproduced exactly; Tódová and Wilkie  extend uplifting to HDR environment maps, and van de Ruit and Eisemann  constrain uplifted spectra by their rendered RGB appearance, including indirect illumination. Guarnera et al.  target illumination spectra specifically, uplifting a light’s tristimulus value by optimising blending weights over a compact spectral basis. They propose two variants: a measured basis of six LED primaries, which produces SPDs with the spectral structure of real multi-primary sources, and a smooth parametric Gaussian basis. Both reproduce the target chromaticity by construction; as with reflectance uplifting, the reconstructed SPD is one metamer of many, and the choice of basis decides which one. Xia et al.  sample the null space of the RGB constraint via differentiable rendering. We benchmark our reflectance upsampler against Jakob and Hanika  and our illumination upsampler against Guarnera et al.  in Sec. . While these methods uplift RGB to $n$ -channel spectra rendered with a spectral renderer, ours map RGB to $k$ -dimensional latent codes rendered with an RGB renderer.()1999()Fascione et al., 2018()2019()Weidlich et al., 2021()2015()2019()Pharr et al., 2023()Jakob et al., 2022()2019()2023(; )20212022()2025()2024()2022()2025()2019()20226.3

    2.4.

    A small but growing line of work delivers spectral phenomena without a spectral renderer. Ward and Eydelberg-Vileshin  prefilter materials and lights before rendering, achieving near-exact direct illumination at the cost of approximate interreflection. Sun  decomposes thin-film iridescence into a small number of RGB passes through an unmodified renderer. Fichet et al.  handle fluorescence by replacing the albedo–light product with a reduced re-radiation matrix, requiring shader-level changes; their reduced-matrix formalism itself is general, and we adopt it in Sec.  to analyse our codec’s constraints. Each of these methods is constructed for a specific phenomenon. We take a different route: a single learned codec supports general spectral transport (reflectance, illumination, coloured glass, conductors, and homogeneous and heterogeneous participating media) through any RGB renderer with no engine modification. Wavelength-shifting effects (fluorescence, phosphorescence, dispersion) couple distinct wavelengths during transport and remain outside the per-channel regime our codec preserves.()2002()2006()20243.4wavelength-preserving

    3.

    Fig.  summarises the system: a jointly trained encoder–decoder pair around otherwise unmodified RGB render passes. This section develops the constraints that shape it.2

    3.1.

    Path tracing repeatedly applies three operations to spectral quantities: scaling (intensity, BSDF evaluation), addition (multiple light contributions, path accumulation), and (Hadamard) multiplication: reflectance with incident radiance, transmittance with through-flux, per-channel attenuation through participating media, and conductor Fresnel evaluated at the complex index $\eta(\lambda)\!-\!i\kappa(\lambda)$ . Discretising the visible spectrum on $n$ wavelength bins yields the algebra $\mathcal{A}=(\mathbb{R}^{n},+,\odot)$ on which transport acts.element-wise1 We use $\kappa$ for the imaginary part of the conductor index to avoid collision with the latent dimension $k$ .11

    A renderer-friendly code must support the same three operations , so that the renderer can treat codes as ordinary $k$ -channel inputs. Formally, this requires the encoder $\mathrm{E}$ to act as a ring homomorphism $\mathcal{A}\to(\mathbb{R}^{k},+,\odot)$ .directly on the compact codes

    3.2.

    The compression we seek does not exist exactly:

    Theorem 3.1.

    When $k

    The argument is that the standard basis $\{e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\}$ forms a system of $n$ pairwise orthogonal nonzero idempotents under $\odot$ , while $(\mathbb{R}^{k},+,\odot)$ admits at most $k$ such idempotents , so for $k(; )Lang, 2002Atiyah and Macdonald, 1969

    The natural relaxation is preservation: scaling and addition are preserved exactly (a property our linear architecture below guarantees by construction), while Hadamard multiplication is preserved approximately on the low-dimensional manifold of natural visible spectra learned from data. The asymmetry is deliberate. Scaling and addition enter every radiance estimate through path accumulation and Monte-Carlo averaging, where a systematic error would bias the estimator itself; the Hadamard product enters once per material interaction, where a small approximation error is perceptually tolerable, and the multi-bounce measurements in Sec.  show that it does not accumulate.distributional6.2

    3.3.

    We instantiate the encoder $\mathrm{E}$ and decoder $\mathrm{D}$ as linear maps

    (1) $z=\mathrm{E}(s)=W_{\mathrm{enc}}\,s,\qquad\hat{s}=\mathrm{D}(z)=W_{\mathrm{dec}}\,z,$

    with $W_{\mathrm{enc}}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}$ and $W_{\mathrm{dec}}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ . Linearity gives $\mathrm{E}(\alpha s)=\alpha\mathrm{E}(s)$ and $\mathrm{E}(s_{1}\!+\!s_{2})=\mathrm{E}(s_{1})+\mathrm{E}(s_{2})$ exactly; only the Hadamard property is learned.

    Both weight matrices are constrained non-negative through a softplus reparameterisation of unconstrained learnable matrices. Non-negativity is essential, not cosmetic: codes of non-negative spectra remain non-negative, so they pack into RGB framebuffers and flow through an unmodified forward-light-only renderer. The columns of $W_{\mathrm{dec}}$ admit a direct interpretation as a basis of spectra, with the latent code being the non-negative mixture-weight vector for that basis.2 Parameterisation details, signed-decoder ablations, and fidelity diagnostics are in Supplemental Sec. 2.22

    3.4.

    Fichet et al.  describe spectral reduction by a pair of maps: an analysis map (our $W_{\mathrm{enc}}$ ) and a reconstruction basis (our $W_{\mathrm{dec}}$ ). In their framework, a material whose spectral action is the diagonal operator $\mathrm{diag}(m)$ , with $m\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq 0}$ the material spectrum, acts on the reduced coefficients through the $k\times k$ ()2024reduced matrix

    (2) $\displaystyle R_{m}$ $\displaystyle=\;W_{\mathrm{enc}}\,\mathrm{diag}(m)\,W_{\mathrm{dec}},$ $\displaystyle(R_{m})_{ij}$ $\displaystyle=\;\sum_{\lambda}W_{\mathrm{enc}}[i,\lambda]\;m(\lambda)\;W_{\mathrm{dec}}[\lambda,j].$

    Applying general reduced matrices requires shader-level matrix–vector products, which is exactly the modification Fichet et al. make. An unmodified RGB renderer can only multiply per channel, so it applies $\mathrm{diag}(z_{m})$ : our setting is the restriction of the reduced-matrix framework to $R_{m}$ .diagonal

    Requiring $(R_{m})_{ij}=0$ for all $i\neq j$ and for non-negative material spectrum $m$ forces each summand in Eq. () to vanish: $W_{\mathrm{enc}}[i,\lambda]\,W_{\mathrm{dec}}[\lambda,j]=0$ at every $\lambda$ , i.e. encoder row $i$ and decoder column $j$ must have disjoint supports for $i\neq j$ . Non-negativity is what makes this rigid: with signed matrices the off-diagonal integral could cancel across wavelengths without the supports being disjoint, whereas non-negative summands admit no cancellation. At the same time, a faithful round-trip requires each encoder row to overlap its decoder column. Exact diagonality for all $m$ therefore forces a partition of the spectrum: each basis function owns a wavelength range, which is precisely binning.every2own

    Binning, however, caps accuracy: the comparison in Sec.  places every pure-binning variant at roughly $3\times$ our error. The codec relaxes exact diagonality to diagonality : the training objective penalises off-diagonal leakage only on products of natural spectra, not for every conceivable $m$ . This relaxation admits learned solutions that binning excludes, and the learning is where the accuracy is earned: in the same comparison, replacing the bin-average encoder with a learned one nearly halves the error of fixed boxes, and learning the decoder jointly nearly halves it again. The learned matrices keep nearly disjoint supports with small, deliberate overlaps (Supplemental Sec. 2). The codec is best understood as the distributionally-diagonal member of the reduced-matrix family that minimises rendered colour error.6.1in distribution

    The codec is : the same $\mathrm{E},\mathrm{D}$ encode reflectance $R$ , illumination $L$ , transmittance $\tau$ , absorption $\sigma_{a}$ and scattering $\sigma_{s}$ coefficients, and the spectral parts of the conductor IOR $\eta,\kappa$ into a common latent space. The learned matrices realise these constraints: the decoder columns are smooth, band-localised spectra with the near-disjoint supports derived above, spanning a chromaticity gamut larger than sRGB on the green, blue and red edges, and the encoder rows are sparser and multi-peaked, acting as band-pass analysers rather than as the transpose of the decoder.content-agnostic

    3.5.

    We choose $k{=}3B$ so the latent code splits into $B$ blocks of three channels. Each block is a triplet; the renderer treats it as an ordinary RGB colour, applies its standard per-channel operations, and writes the output to the corresponding block of an HDR framebuffer. The full $k$ -dimensional code is processed in $B$ unmodified RGB passes. For two spectra $s_{R},s_{L}$ encoded as $z_{R},z_{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ the renderer computes

    (3) $z_{R}\odot z_{L}\;=\;\bigoplus_{b=1}^{B}\!\bigl(z_{R}^{(b)}\!\odot\,z_{L}^{(b)}\bigr),$

    with $z^{(b)}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{3}$ the $b$ -th triplet and $\bigoplus$ concatenation. Eq. () introduces no new operation: it is the same $\odot$ on a $k$ -vector, written to expose the renderer’s per-pass three-channel structure. The training objective, defined next, drives the codec toward3

    (4) $\mathrm{E}(s_{R}\odot s_{L})\;\approx\;\mathrm{E}(s_{R})\odot\mathrm{E}(s_{L}),$

    on the data manifold, so the per-pass product the renderer computes matches the encoded product of the spectral interaction.

    3.6.

    The codec is trained on a corpus of measured and synthetic reflectance spectra (Munsell extended to sRGB-edge coverage) and an augmented illumination corpus (LSPDD-measured lamps , CIE daylight, and synthetic narrowband variants, prefiltered by bin integration so that mercury lines and other narrow peaks survive downsampling). Full corpus construction, split methodology, and representative test spectra are in Supplemental Sec. 3.3.()LSPDD, 2026

    The codec minimises

    (5) $\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{\mathrm{e2e}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{e2e}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{rec}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{code}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{code}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{col}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{col}},$

    each term targeting one component of the spectral pipeline:

    $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{e2e}}$ $\displaystyle=\Phi\bigl(\mathrm{D}(\mathrm{E}(R)\odot\mathrm{E}(L)),\;R\odot L\bigr)$ $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}$ $\displaystyle=\mathrm{MSE}(\mathrm{D}\mathrm{E}R,\,R)+\mathrm{MSE}(\mathrm{D}\mathrm{E}L,\,L)$ $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{code}}$ $\displaystyle=\mathrm{MSE}\bigl(\mathrm{E}(R)\odot\mathrm{E}(L),\;\mathrm{E}(R\odot L)\bigr)$ $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{col}}$ $\displaystyle=\Delta E_{76}\bigl(\mathrm{D}(\mathrm{E}(R)\odot\mathrm{E}(L)),\;R\odot L\bigr).$

    $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{e2e}}$ is the end-to-end fit between the codec-rendered product and the spectral ground truth, with $\Phi(x,y)=(2-\cos(x,y))\,\mathrm{MSE}(x,y)$ combining magnitude and shape. $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}$ enforces round-trip accuracy on individual spectra. $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{code}}$ is the Hadamard-multiplicativity term that Theorem  forbids from reaching zero in general but that we minimise in distribution. $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{col}}$ evaluates the same product–ground-truth pair as $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{e2e}}$ , but perceptually: as $\Delta E_{76}$ in CIELAB under the per-sample illuminant white point. $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{code}}$ alone admits the trivial collapse $\mathrm{E}\equiv 0$ ; $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{e2e}}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}$ make this infeasible by requiring the codec to reproduce both individual spectra and their products. The same argument pins the overall scale: rescaling $\mathrm{E}\!\to\!s\mathrm{E}$ and $\mathrm{D}\!\to\!\mathrm{D}/s$ leaves $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}$ unchanged, but $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{e2e}}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{col}}$ apply the encoder twice and the decoder once, so their error grows as $s$ shrinks and the degeneracy is excluded. Non-negativity is enforced architecturally by the softplus parameterisation and needs no penalty.3.1

    Eq. () trains on single reflectance–illuminant products; it is $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{code}}$ that trains the latent product structure which iterates over multiple bounces, and multi-bounce accuracy is measured empirically (Sec. ). The corpus contains reflectance and illumination spectra only; transmittance, complex IOR, and scattering coefficients are encoded with the same matrices, without retraining (Sec. ).56.24

    The four weights $\lambda_{\bullet}$ were selected by a two-phase random search over 130 codec variants, optimising for stability under chained products (three or more spectra, i.e. multiple rendering bounces); the search ranked candidates by $\Delta E_{94}$ for speed, while all reported results use $\Delta E_{2000}$ . The selected values, the search protocol, and the multi-bounce sensitivity sweep are in Supplemental Sec. 3.2.

    4.

    The codec compresses any visible-range spectral quantity the same way (Sec. ): whichever spectral input a BSDF or volume model expects (reflectance, transmittance, complex index of refraction, absorption or scattering coefficients) is encoded once into a $k$ -dimensional latent code and processed by the unmodified renderer in $B{=}k/3$ standard RGB passes. The renderer’s per-channel arithmetic (scaling, addition, Hadamard products at material interactions, and per-channel attenuation through participating media) operates on the $k$ latent channels exactly as it would on three RGB channels.3.1

    Coloured glass.

    Coloured glass is characterised by a wavelength-dependent transmittance $\tau(\lambda)\!\in\![0,1]$ that attenuates light passing through it. We handle two physically distinct regimes. For thin filters and surface coatings, the transmittance acts as a per-crossing multiplier on the radiance: at each interface $L_{\mathrm{out}}(\lambda)\!=\!\tau(\lambda)\,L_{\mathrm{in}}(\lambda)$ . Encoding $z_{\tau}\!=\!\mathrm{E}(\tau)$ once and applying $z_{\tau}^{(b)}$ per channel across $N$ surface crossings corresponds to integer Hadamard powers $z_{\tau}^{N}$ , the iterated-product structure the codec is trained to approximate. For bulk-absorbing glass, spectral attenuation follows the Beer–Lambert law along the optical path: $T(d,\lambda)\!=\!\exp(-\sigma_{a}(\lambda)\,d)$ . We obtain a latent absorption coefficient by inverting the encoded transmittance at a reference depth, $\sigma_{a}^{(b)}\!=\!-\ln(z_{\tau}^{(b)})/d_{\mathrm{ref}}$ ; the renderer’s per-channel volume integrator then applies $\exp(-\sigma_{a}^{(b)}\,d)$ along each ray segment of length $d$ , a fractional Hadamard power the codec approximates.

    Conductors.

    A conductor BSDF is parameterised by a wavelength-dependent complex index of refraction $\eta(\lambda)\!-\!i\kappa(\lambda)$ . We encode $\eta$ and $\kappa$ through the same codec, recovering two $k$ -dimensional codes $z_{\eta},z_{\kappa}$ , and feed them per-pass to the unmodified conductor BSDF. The Fresnel equations are non-linear in $\eta,\kappa$ , but the non-linearity acts : the renderer evaluates Fresnel on the $k$ latent channels just as it would on three RGB channels. Replacing one accurate spectral Fresnel evaluation with $k$ approximate per-channel ones is far less lossy than the standard RGB collapse because the $k$ near-disjoint latent channels sample $\eta$ and $\kappa$ much more finely than three broad RGB primaries. The renderer remains an opaque RGB BSDF evaluator; the spectral information lives in the latent channels alone.as ordinary spectraper channel3 Per-channel Fresnel evaluation on RGB primaries is known to distort metal colours ; the encoding applies equally when the renderer uses the Schlick approximation.33()Hoffman, 2019

    Homogeneous participating media.

    Absorption $\sigma_{a}(\lambda)$ and scattering $\sigma_{s}(\lambda)$ coefficients are ordinary non-negative visible-range spectra, which the codec embeds directly. We encode each separately, and the renderer’s standard per-channel volume integrator (the same code path it uses for an RGB homogeneous medium) accumulates per-channel transmittance $\exp(-(\sigma_{a}^{(b)}\!+\!\sigma_{s}^{(b)})\,d)$ and applies the single-scatter albedo $\sigma_{s}^{(b)}/(\sigma_{a}^{(b)}\!+\!\sigma_{s}^{(b)})$ as a per-channel multiplier at scattering events, the transport that produces subsurface scattering (SSS) in translucent materials. Media therefore exercise two per-channel regimes: extinction follows the Beer–Lambert analysis above, and the scattering albedo is a per-channel ratio of two encoded spectra. The same codec, trained on reflectance and illumination only, encodes extinction coefficients without retraining. For media with strongly saturated absorption bands, whose albedo the ratio regime cannot represent accurately, we factor the transmittance into a per-crossing chromatic term, encoded as a surface transmittance, and a smooth residual absorption coefficient carried by the medium.

    Heterogeneous participating media.

    Per-voxel spectral data is encoded into the same $k$ -dimensional latent space and stored as $B$ RGB-format grid volumes; each pass reads its triplet through the renderer’s heterogeneous-medium machinery without modification. Linearity of the encoder makes this both practical and exact. Voxel spectra are typically blends of a few feature spectra, and encoding commutes with blending: the feature spectra are encoded once and their latent codes blended per voxel, so no per-voxel encoding is needed, and the renderer’s volume filtering commutes with the encoding for the same reason (exactly so for trilinear and any non-negative linear filter). Along a ray, the accumulated optical depth is a per-channel sum of voxel contributions, and sums are preserved exactly, as is rescaling by a scalar density field, which multiplies all channels by the same factor. Heterogeneity therefore introduces no approximation beyond the homogeneous regimes above: the deviation remains that of the per-channel exponential and the albedo ratio.

    Per-class encoding parameters and renderer bindings are documented in Supplemental Sec. 6.

    5.

    While our codec compresses spectral inputs end-to-end, production pipelines hold large libraries of RGB textures, materials, and environment maps for which spectral data is unavailable. The obvious route for such assets is to uplift them with an existing RGB-to-spectrum method, for example Jakob and Hanika , and encode the result. This composes two independent approximations: the uplift selects one metamer with no regard for the codec, and the encoder then compresses a spectrum that need not lie near its training distribution. We instead train lightweight networks that map the RGB input directly to a latent code. The prediction target is the code the codec itself would produce for the underlying spectrum, so the networks learn to land on codes that render accurately: on held-out data the composed route yields about $1.6\times$ the colour error of direct prediction (the through-codec baseline rows of Tab. ), while direct prediction stays close to the codec’s own accuracy on ground-truth spectra. The upsamplers are a convenience bridge for RGB-only assets, not a spectral reconstruction method.()20195

    Both networks map a colour input $\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ to a $k$ -dimensional latent code:

    (6) $z_{\mathrm{pred}}=\begin{cases}f^{(\mathrm{R})}_{\theta}(\mathbf{c})&\text{(reflectance assets)}\\ f^{(\mathrm{L})}_{\phi}(\mathbf{c})&\text{(illumination assets).}\end{cases}$

    The networks operate in linear XYZ: at training time the input is the CMF projection of the training spectrum, and at render time RGB assets are first linearised and converted with the standard sRGB-to-XYZ matrix. We use two networks rather than one because reflectance distributions are bounded ( $s\in[0,1]^{n}$ ) and broadly Munsell-like, whereas illumination is unbounded and includes narrowband emission peaks; the two need different inductive biases. Both networks are per-pixel multilayer perceptrons with scale equivariance (the input magnitude is factored out, the network maps the unit direction to a unit-scale latent, and the magnitude is reapplied at the output) so the codec’s exact scale equivariance carries through to RGB inputs. The reflectance network additionally has an , a small MLP that decodes the predicted latent back to a reconstructed spectrum, supervised by a smoothness penalty during training. This auxiliary path acts as a regulariser tied to the smooth Munsell-like prior of reflectance and improves reflectance accuracy by $2.5\times$ (Supplemental Sec. 7); we find no equivalent benefit for illumination, whose narrowband peaks penalise smoothness, so $f^{(\mathrm{L})}$ uses a single latent head. Codec weights are frozen during upsampler training.auxiliary spectrum head

    Training objective.

    For each spectrum $s$ in the codec’s training set the input is the CMF projection $\mathbf{c}=T_{\mathrm{cmf}}\,s$ and the target latent is $z_{\mathrm{gt}}=\mathrm{E}(s)$ . Both networks share a common latent-supervision loss

    (7) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{lat}}={}$ $\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}\bigl(z_{\mathrm{pred}},z_{\mathrm{gt}}\bigr)$ $\displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{maxabs}}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|z_{\mathrm{pred}}-z_{\mathrm{gt}}\|_{\infty}\bigr]$ $\displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{col}}\,\Delta E_{76}\bigl(\mathrm{D}(z_{\mathrm{pred}}),\mathrm{D}(z_{\mathrm{gt}})\bigr),$

    where the MSE enforces overall latent accuracy, the $\ell_{\infty}$ term controls outlier dimensions, and the perceptual $\Delta E_{76}$ term, computed on the decoded spectra in CIELAB, ensures colorimetric stability after decode. The reflectance network additionally supervises its spectrum-head output $\hat{s}_{\mathrm{pred}}$ against the ground-truth spectrum: $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{spec}}^{(\mathrm{R})}=\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{s}_{\mathrm{pred}},s)+\lambda_{\mathrm{smooth}}\,\sum_{i}(\hat{s}_{i+1}-\hat{s}_{i})^{2}$ , yielding the total reflectance loss $\mathcal{L}^{(\mathrm{R})}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{lat}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{spec}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{spec}}^{(\mathrm{R})}$ . Loss weights and training schedule are in Supplemental Sec. 7.

    Scope.

    Three boundaries delimit what these networks do. First, RGB-to-spectrum upsampling is one-to-many: a colour corresponds to many metamers, and a deterministic network selects a single one. Like all one-to-one upsamplers, ours does not address metamerism; when an asset’s true spectrum differs from the selected metamer, relighting can diverge, and smooth selections are the safer choice. We therefore claim no recovery of true spectra: the target is a latent code that reproduces the asset’s colour and renders robustly across illuminants. Second, unlike methods that enforce the input colour as a hard constraint, our round-trip is soft: Eq. () penalises but does not eliminate colour drift. The cost is small on reflectances (Supplemental Sec. 7) and is most visible under broadband illumination upsampling, where a hard-constrained uplift is close to exact by construction (Tab. ); in exchange, the soft formulation is free to trade exact colour reproduction at one condition for rendering accuracy across conditions. Third, scale equivariance is the correct prior for illumination, whose overall intensity is arbitrary, but for reflectance it forgoes the brightness information that recent uplift methods exploit to constrain the feasible metamer set; we accept this trade for a single shared mechanism across both asset types.75

    Application: spectral assets from RGB inputs.

    At render time, RGB textures and environment maps are upsampled per pixel into a $k$ -dimensional latent map, packed as $k/3$ RGB-format EXR textures, and rendered through the unmodified renderer (Sec. ).6.3

    6.

    We evaluate the codec against spectral rendering as ground truth (Mitsuba 0.6 spectral build) and against standard RGB rendering as the practical baseline (the same Mitsuba 0.6 in RGB mode; the spectral build is never touched by our pipeline). We use $k{=}6$ (two RGB passes) throughout. All qualitative figures decode latents to spectra and CMF-integrate to sRGB. Sample budgets vary per scene class to balance Monte-Carlo noise against render time and are stated per figure; further tables and ablations are in the supplemental material.

    6.1.

    Cornell-box evaluation under five illuminants.

    We first evaluate the codec at $k{=}6$ on a Cornell box containing diverse BRDFs and a ColorChecker chart, rendered under broadband, narrowband, structured, and multi-peaked illumination (Fig. ; per-condition values in the figure). Materials and illuminants here are spectral ground truth encoded directly through the codec, with no upsampling involved. Across all five illuminants the latent pipeline reduces $\overline{\Delta E}_{2000}$ vs. spectral ground truth by $1.6$ – $4.4\times$ over standard RGB rendering; the advantage is largest under the structured red-dominant source narrow ( $0.86$ vs. $3.82$ ) and warm daylight ( $0.90$ vs. $3.40$ ). A 52-cell sweep over Gaussian-narrowband illuminants (13 centres $\times$ 4 FWHMs spanning the visible band) gives a mean per-cell codec advantage of $11.2\times$ over RGB (Supplemental Sec. 5).3351

    Capacity and binning baselines.

    Since the learned decoder has nearly disjoint supports (Sec. ), a natural question is whether plain wavelength binning at $k{=}6$ would suffice. It does not. Tab.  evaluates the full ladder on the same Cornell-box suite (illuminant SPDs in Fig. ): three pure binning variants (bin-average encoder, box decoder, no training), the two half-learned bases (fixed decoder shape, trained encoder), and the jointly learned codec.3.414

    Averaged over the five illuminants, every binning variant, including bins placed at our own decoder’s transitions, is about $3\times$ less accurate than the learned codec and worse than plain RGB. The two narrowband columns expose why: binning accuracy depends on how the source’s spectral structure falls relative to the fixed bin edges. The same adaptive bins score $1.33$ when the $525$  nm Gaussian lands near a bin centre and $6.69$ on narrow, whose red-dominant multi-lobed spectrum straddles several bin edges, and no placement resolves FL11’s three emission peaks ( $5.0$ – $5.6$ vs. our $1.8$ ). The codec is placement-robust ( $1.11$ and $0.86$ ) and remains the most accurate representation even in the binning-friendly $525$  nm column. Nor is the decoder shape the whole contribution: on the same equal-width boxes, learning only the encoder cuts the average error nearly in half ( $4.35\!\to\!2.36$ ), and jointly learning the decoder nearly halves it again ( $\to\!1.24$ ). The half-learned bases also expose a robustness failure the joint codec avoids: each is competitive on smooth broadband light but collapses on a different structured cell (boxes at $2.94$ on the $525$  nm source and $4.14$ on FL11, Gaussians at $7.52$ on FL11). The near-disjoint decoder is an outcome of the joint optimisation, not evidence that a box basis suffices. Fig.  shows the corresponding renders and error maps under FL11, the column where the differences are largest. PCA and NMF baselines and further per-illuminant breakdowns are in Supplemental Sec. 4.3515

    Capacity at $k{=}6$ vs. $k{=}9$ .

    A 13-scene cross-class sweep (the four Cornell-box illuminants, three coloured glasses, three measured conductors, and three subsurface materials) gives an aggregate $\overline{\Delta E}_{2000}$ difference of $-0.05$ in favour of $k{=}9$ ; the gain is negligible, and per-scene differences trade in both directions rather than favouring either setting systematically (Supplemental Sec. 4.4, which also examines why the gain saturates). At $50\%$ extra rendering cost this is not a favourable trade; we use $k{=}6$ throughout.

    6.2.

    We evaluate the codec on the material classes of Sec.  with one scene per material, the XYZ RGB Inc. dragon (the heterogeneous SSS case uses a hand volume): coloured glass in the surface and Beer–Lambert regimes, subsurface scattering in the dipole and homogeneous regimes, measured conductors, and a heterogeneous volume. All scenes use the same $k{=}6$ codec under D65; the reference is Mitsuba 0.6’s spectral build. We report the object-masked mean $\Delta E_{2000}$ against the reference after matching each candidate’s mean luminance to it on the mask; the remaining materials of each class are in Supplemental Sec. 6.4.4

    Coloured glass.

    We evaluate five Schott filters (OG550, RG610, and GG495 longpass; BG7 and VG9 bandpass) in both regimes (Supplemental Sec. 6 renders the set as hollow vases; Fig.  shows OG550, BG7, and RG610): a thin transmittance filter on the dragon surface, and Beer–Lambert absorption through the solid body. Tab.  reports dragon-masked $\Delta E_{2000}$ at 1024 spp.62

    OG550 shows the largest gain in both regimes: RGB cannot represent its sharp mid-visible cutoff. The smallest gains come from VG9 and RG610, whose spectra RGB approximates least badly.

    Subsurface scattering.

    We compare the two subsurface regimes, dipole BSSRDF and homogeneous medium, side by side (Sec. ; yellow-green dipole, skin, and wine homogeneous in Fig. ; pale mint, rose, and potato dipole in Supplemental Sec. 6.4). Homogeneous dragons encode spectral $\sigma_{a}(\lambda),\sigma_{s}(\lambda)$ (a spectral skin profile and the red-wine coefficients of the teaser scene) through the unmodified renderer’s per-channel volume integrator; dipole dragons encode custom chromophore-band RGB $\sigma$ targets (their names describe the resulting appearance), smooth-upsampled to spectra and codec-encoded. Tab.  reports dragon-masked $\Delta E_{2000}$ at 1024 spp (dipole) and 4096 spp (homogeneous).463

    The codec advantage is largest on saturated chromophore-band materials (wine, yellow-green) and smallest on near-broadband translucents (potato, pale mint), where the RGB baseline already captures the appearance reasonably.

    Heterogeneous subsurface scattering.

    We render a per-voxel spectral hand volume through the renderer’s heterogeneous-medium machinery (Fig. ). The albedo is built from five anatomical features (baseline skin, freckles, knuckles, fingertips, veins) blended over the geometry; the warm features are lifted to spectra via Gitlina et al.’s skin reflectance LUT , and the vein target via a chromaticity-faithful basis fit  since it sits outside the skin gamut (construction details in Supplemental Sec. 6.3). At 4096 spp the codec attains mean $\Delta E_{2000}\!=\!0.93$ over the hand silhouette against $4.00$ for the RGB baseline through the same volume (p95 $1.89$ vs. $6.62$ ), a $4.29\times$ gain. The advantage spans the whole visible surface: the RGB baseline’s error map is substantially higher across the hand, and highest on the fingers, knuckles, and veins (Fig. ). The heterogeneous advantage is geometry-bounded: it grows with the optical path length through coloured material, so it is most pronounced on solid bodies and muted on thin shells.7()2020()Guarnera et al., 20227

    Conductors.

    We render five measured conductors (silver, gold, copper, aluminium, chromium) as a solid dragon under D65 (renders for the first three in Fig. ). Reflectance on a conductor is a smooth but spectrally non-trivial Fresnel function of two complex IOR spectra, which the standard RGB pipeline must collapse to a single three-channel reflectance; the codec instead preserves the encoded $\eta,\kappa$ pair and computes the Fresnel response per pass (Sec. ; renderer bindings and a mirror-based variant in Supplemental Sec. 6.1). Tab.  reports dragon-masked $\Delta E_{2000}$ at 1024 spp.844

    Most of the RGB baseline’s error is a magnitude error: collapsing the complex IOR to a three-channel Fresnel overestimates conductor reflectance by roughly a factor of two before brightness matching, with a residual hue shift for the coloured metals (gold, copper) and almost none for silver, whose spectral Fresnel is nearly neutral. The $\Delta E_{2000}$ maps saturate across the entire dragon silhouette for the RGB baseline while the latent column stays uniformly low (Fig. ).8

    Multi-bounce stability.

    On the Mitsuba test scene (Supplemental Sec. 2.4) under broadband and FL11 illumination, per-pixel error stabilises immediately: from direct lighting to one bounce the mean $\Delta E_{2000}$ rises by at most $0.02$ , then remains flat through $32$ bounces (the maximum tested) at $0.91/1.62$ (broadband) and $1.32/1.93$ (FL11) for mean/p95. The approximate Hadamard product does not accumulate at any depth; the codec self-product check in Supplemental Sec. 2.3 corroborates this.matpreview

    Approximation behaviour.

    Each per-channel regime of Sec.  replaces an exact spectral operation with a latent one. The bounds that follow are worst-case by construction: the stress chains iterate a single encoded spectrum, whereas real paths mix different surfaces whose encoding errors partially cancel, so rendered scene means sit at the foot of the curves. Even so, the deviations are bounded and slow-growing: repeated self-products of the same encoded spectrum stay below a $\Delta E_{2000}$ of $5$ through twelve surface crossings; Beer–Lambert transmittance error rises from the codec’s product floor ( $0.96$ ) to $1$ – $6$ at the reference depth; per-channel conductor Fresnel is nearly angle-independent below $60^{\circ}$ , adding about two units at grazing incidence; and the single-scatter albedo ratio stays below $6$ through twenty scattering orders for smooth subsurface materials, while saturated media use the factorised encoding. The characterisation curves, evaluated exactly as the pipeline operates and overlaid with the rendered scene means of this section, are in Supplemental Sec. 6.5.4

    6.3.

    Per-spectrum upsampling accuracy.

    For each test reflectance $R$ and illuminant $L$ we compare the rendered radiance $\hat{R}\,L$ (or $R\,\hat{L}$ ) against the spectral ground truth $R\,L$ in CIELAB with $L$ ’s own integrated white point. Tab.  reports $\Delta E_{2000}$ across 218 held-out reflectances and four CIE illuminants for both upsampling directions. Rows are grouped by what the route asks of the renderer, because the baselines are spectral methods: each uplifts an RGB asset to a full spectrum, which a spectral renderer then transports. That is the capability our setting assumes is unavailable, so those rows are context rather than a comparison with ours. Encoding the same uplifted spectrum and rendering it in two RGB passes puts every method in the pipeline we target, and it is those groups that compare like with like. The bottom row applies the codec directly to ground-truth spectra and serves as the no-upsampling reference.5

    Four observations follow from Tab. . First, on the reflectance side the uplifting baselines are the most accurate under D65, which is their construction point: each is fitted to reproduce the target colour under the illuminant its fit is anchored to, and drifts as the illuminant departs from it, so their tails grow sharply under the structured sources while the latent path stays bounded. Second, this anchoring is most visible in the basis fit of Guarnera et al. : designed for illumination, it reproduces its calibration point almost exactly, and the same fit applied to reflectance drifts further as the illuminant departs from it. Third, on the illumination side the comparison splits by illuminant: the scaled uplift is the more accurate under D65, the two are within $0.1$ under FL11, and our upsampler is the most accurate under both LED sources, where it also undercuts the ground-truth-spectra reference. Fourth, uplifting to a spectrum and then encoding composes two approximations, at a measurable cost against predicting the code directly ( $2.24$ against $1.38$ on average); the direct route exists to avoid that composition. The reflectance upsampler’s mean signed CIELAB offset matches the no-upsampling reference on every illuminant, and is smaller than the uplift-then-encode route’s on all four (Supplemental Sec. 7). Robustness beyond these four sources is probed next.5()2022

    Measured lamps.

    To probe illumination robustness beyond the four CIE illuminants of Tab. , we evaluate the same per-spectrum pipeline on 48 measured commercial and standard lamps (LSPDD compact-fluorescent, metal-halide, and high-pressure sodium sources plus the CIE FL and HP series, none in the training corpus). Tab.  separates two questions. First, the representation itself holds up on unseen spectra: encoded directly, the codec stays close to its in-distribution accuracy across the whole population, while a pipeline with no spectral representation is several times less accurate. Second, recovery from RGB alone is a harder problem: the worst cases are the structured discharge lamps, and it is there that the routes separate, the latent upsampler having the lower error on all 48 lamps against the basis fit of Guarnera et al. and on 37 of 48 against the scaled uplift, the exceptions being fluorescent standards where the two are comparable. The same population tests the reflectance side: across the 48 lamps the direct route is more accurate than uplift-then-encode on every one.5()LSPDD, 20266

    Spectral environment maps.

    Finally, we render the upsamplers (Sec. ) in complete scenes: Cornell boxes lit by measured hyperspectral environment maps  (Fig. ), pairing each baseline with the corresponding route of ours, Jakob and Hanika  against $f^{(\mathrm{R})}$ with a ground-truth envmap, and Guarnera et al.’s 6-LED basis  against $f^{(\mathrm{L})}$ with ground-truth materials. Per-cell values are in the figure. As in Tab. , the two baselines are rendered spectrally and carry uplift error only, while every column of ours is the deployable two-pass route and carries the codec’s error as well. “Codec, $k{=}6$ ” applies the codec to ground-truth spectra and bounds what upsampling can achieve in these scenes. In the two maps the rendered routes are indistinguishable.5()Morimoto et al., 20199()2019()20225

    6.4.

    To verify that the codec deploys without renderer modification, we run it through four production frameworks: Blender Cycles (open-source path tracer; broadband and narrowband conditions), Autodesk Maya with Arnold (offline production), KeyShot (envmap-driven product visualisation), and Unreal Engine 5 (real-time rasteriser with Lumen global illumination). In each pipeline the latent code is treated as RGB material textures and light SPDs over two passes, and the decoder is a matrix multiply on the pass outputs.

    Spectral ground truth is not natively available in these commercial pipelines, so we construct one per renderer: every material is uplifted to a spectrum with Jakob and Hanika  (the reference is not built with our codec), light sources use their known SPDs, and each scene is rendered in 16 RGB-packed passes that reconstruct the full spectrum, stored as linear floating-point data with per-renderer response and exposure calibration (KeyShot and Cycles at 128 spp, Arnold at AA level 3, Unreal via the Movie Render Queue; configurations in Supplemental Sec. 9). Against this reference we evaluate three routes per scene (Figs. –): the codec applied to the same spectral assets in two RGB passes, which isolates the codec’s own error in each pipeline; the full RGB-asset route through our upsamplers, which adds the recovery cost; and the renderer’s plain RGB baseline.()20191013

    Across the thirteen scene and lighting cases the codec’s own error stays below $2.8\,\Delta E_{2000}$ in every renderer and lighting condition, the RGB-asset route adds a bounded upsampling premium, largest under Unreal’s deliberately metameric lighting, and the plain RGB baseline is the least accurate of the three in twelve of the thirteen cases. The exception is a nearly flat broadband source in Maya, smoother across the visible band than D65, under which all three routes fall within $2\,\Delta E_{2000}$ of the reference. Per-case means and 95th percentiles are in Supplemental Sec. 9. KeyShot is evaluated both under its environment map and under uniform-colour environment lights carrying the same known SPDs as the Maya cases; the RGB pipelines are the renderers’ own linear outputs, brightness-matched to the reference.

    A 120-frame animated sequence in Blender Cycles confirms temporal stability: no flicker or chromatic drift across either broadband or narrowband condition (per-renderer configurations and the supplemental video are in Supplemental Sec. 9).

    6.5.

    At $k{=}6$ our method requires two RGB render passes, so its per-frame cost is about twice an RGB render by construction and comparable to a modern spectral renderer with hero wavelength sampling . We benchmark end-to-end, including codec encode and decode, against Mitsuba 3’s spectral path tracer at matched resolution and spp (Fig. , Tab. ; full configurations in Supplemental Sec. 8).()Wilkie et al., 2014147

    On the Cornell box the two-pass pipeline is at parity: within $\pm 10\%$ on 14 of 15 resolution and spp configurations, median $+5\%$ , one at $+20\%$ . On heavier scenes the ratio depends on how much of the frame time is wavelength-dependent shading rather than geometry traversal: near parity where shading dominates, up to $1.8\times$ on a textured interior dominated by traversal, and adding spectral load to that same interior narrows the gap. Reconstruction quality across the same spp and resolution sweep is reported in Supplemental Sec. 8. Decoding is a single matrix multiply on the framebuffer and stays below $0.5\%$ of frame time at 1024 spp and above.

    7.

    We introduced a learned linear non-negative spectral codec that compresses spectra into $k$ -dimensional spectral codes, exactly preserving scaling and addition and approximately preserving the per-channel product on which renderer shading operates. At equal $k$ , the learned basis is consistently more accurate than binning: on the Cornell box every binning variant is about $3\times$ less accurate, learning the encoder over fixed boxes nearly halves the error, and jointly learning the decoder nearly halves it again (Sec. ). At $k{=}6$ , two unmodified RGB passes through any path tracer reconstruct a spectral image to a mean $\Delta E_{2000}$ between $0.7$ and $2.7$ (median $1.8$ ) of the spectral ground truth across coloured glass, conductors, dipole and homogeneous subsurface scattering, and a per-voxel heterogeneous subsurface-scattering hand (Sec. ); end-to-end wall-clock time is at near parity with Mitsuba 3’s hero wavelength sampling on shading-bound scenes and about $1.8\times$ on a traversal-bound interior (Sec. ). Legacy RGB assets enter the same pipeline through small XYZ-conditioned upsampling networks that add a bounded premium over the no-upsampling reference (Sec. ). Deployment is renderer-agnostic: we drove four production engines, Blender Cycles, Maya Arnold, KeyShot, and Unreal Engine 5, through the same two-pass interface unmodified, recovering colour information the RGB pipeline collapses. The renderer never changes; only the meaning of its three channels does. This is efficient .6.16.26.56.3spectral rendering without a spectral renderer

    Scope.

    The codec preserves only what reduces to per-channel arithmetic. Wavelength-shifting phenomena couple distinct wavelengths during transport and cannot be captured by a per-channel $\odot$ regardless of $k$ : fluorescence, phosphorescence, and the chromatic dispersion that arises from a wavelength-dependent index of refraction. BSDF non-linearities that escape per-channel arithmetic (e.g. a coated layer whose internal Fresnel contains $\exp(-\sigma\,d)$ along a wavelength-dependent path) similarly fall outside the supported regime; Sec.  enumerates the cases that are inside it. Layered materials, whose cross-layer coupling is non-linear in the spectra, are a natural target for future work under the same constraint. Residual error is largest under extremely peaked illuminants and after many indirect interactions, but Sec.  shows it stabilises with bounce count rather than diverging. The advantage is concentrated where an RGB pipeline discards spectral information. On spectrally bland media and under smooth broadband light the RGB baseline loses little, and the codec’s own reconstruction floor of one to two $\Delta E_{2000}$ units can match or exceed it, as in the broadband Maya case of Sec. . For effects outside the regime, the codec is a pre-encoder for the linear part of the pipeline and would need to be paired with a renderer-side handler for the non-linear residual.46.26.4

    Three practical boundaries follow from the construction. The codec operates on the 400–700 nm band; energy outside it contributes little to CMF-integrated colour, and extending the wavelength grid requires only retraining on a wider corpus, not an architectural change. The two passes must remain linear until decode: tone mapping or other non-linear frame operations on the per-pass buffers before decoding would break the product algebra, so decoding must precede any such post-processing. Finally, the encoder weights wavelengths non-uniformly, so near-monochromatic sources at adjacent wavelengths can encode at different magnitudes; accuracy on measured and held-out lamps is unaffected, and the effect is confined to near-monochromatic light (Supplemental Sec. 5).

    This work was partly supported by the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) grant AH/Y001079/1 (CoSTAR Live Lab).

item.title: The Double-Edged Sword of Open-Ended Interaction: How LLM-Driven NPCs Affect Players' Cognitive Load and Gaming Experience
item.description:

PDF：https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.10107v3

命中：npc

This study examines how large language model-driven non-player characters (LLM-NPCs) affect players' cognitive load and gaming experience, with a particular focus on the underlying psychological mechanisms, differences across task scenarios, and the role of individual traits. Conducting a randomized between-subject experiment (N=130) in a self-developed game prototype "Campus Culture Week", we com

[Submitted on 11 Apr 2026 (), last revised 18 Oct 2026 (this version, v3)]v1

Title:

, , , , Authors:Ting-Chen HsuWenran ChenJiangxu LinFei QinZheyuan ZhangView PDF
This study examines how large language model-driven non-player characters (LLM-NPCs) affect players' cognitive load and gaming experience, with a particular focus on the underlying psychological mechanisms, differences across task scenarios, and the role of individual traits. Conducting a randomized between-subject experiment (N=130) in a self-developed game prototype "Campus Culture Week", we compared player interactions with LLM-NPCs and traditional pre-scripted NPCs across multiple interactive modules. The results showed that the LLM-NPC condition, which combined free-form natural-language input with LLM-generated responses, produced higher cognitive load than preset-option scripted NPC interaction (p < .001), with expressive effort and response uncertainty as significant mediating pathways. However, LLM-NPCs did not yield a statistically significant improvement in overall gaming experience (p = .195); while they positively influenced players' perceived autonomy, they exerted a negative influence on system usability and trust. The effects of LLM-NPCs also significantly varied across task scenarios (p < .001), with stronger increases in cognitive load in more open-ended modules such as content creation and relationship building. The influence of individual differences was generally limited, with no robust associations remaining after correction for multiple comparisons. This study provides empirical evidence for understanding the "double-edged sword" effect of LLM-NPCs on player experience, and highlights the importance of scenario-sensitive and user-sensitive design in intelligent NPC systems. Abstract:

AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents

MirroS Technical Report October 8, 2026

Abstract

Interactive virtual worlds allow agents to learn through exploration and interaction. What agents can learn is bounded by the environments they practice in, which must be , with consistent state, rules, and dynamics, and , with observations that follow the real-world visual distributions. Achieving both across diverse worlds remains a bottleneck. We introduce , a framework that couples simulators and game engines with a shared to build real-time interactive environments. Its simulation backends maintain persistent world state and execute program-defined interaction rules, while the renderer generates visual observations from structured conditions exported through a common interface. To build the neural renderer, we adapt a pretrained video model to geometry conditions, distill it with our proposed , and optimize inference for real-time interaction. Adversarial Forcing makes history prefilling differentiable through exact replay, so that losses on later predictions update how the renderer encodes prior observations, and adds real-data adversarial supervision to improve its visual quality. In AgentGarten, agents perceive the world through visual observations, interact with it in real time, and improve by distilling each round of experience into playbooks that subsequent agents inherit and refine. Our empirical study demonstrates a substantial gain in learning efficiency, with agents learning from just 4 rounds compared with millions for a conventional reinforcement learning counterpart. As new worlds can be written as code and rendered through the same interface, environments can scale in both number and difficulty alongside their agents, a step toward agents that keep evolving through interactive experience.faithfulrealisticAgentGartenneural rendererAdversarial Forcing

Agents learn from trajectories of actions and observations. Developing scalable, generalizable agent capabilities requires environments that not only faithfully preserve the consequences of past actions over extended interactions, but also support flexible variation in layouts, objects, and task rules. Across navigation, manipulation, and multi-agent interaction, scaling these environments therefore requires both controllable, inspectable dynamics and diverse visual observations.

However, existing approaches face a fundamental trade-off. Simulators and game engines support agent learning through explicit state and programmable interaction rules . Yet expanding their visual diversity entails substantial 3D asset creation and complex rendering pipelines, making new environments costly to build and customize. Conversely, video world models synthesize rich, interactive visual observations from data . In these models, however, task-relevant state and physical transition rules remain implicit within generated histories and learned representations, precluding direct inspection, editing, and testing of the environment’s behavior.[, , ]123[, , , ]4567

We introduce , a framework for building that combines programmable dynamics with a shared, real-time neural renderer (Figure ). In AgentGarten, each scene program runs in a simulator or game engine that maintains persistent state and executes explicit interaction rules. A shared neural renderer synthesizes the agent’s visual observations from structured conditions exported by the engine through a unified interface. This separation preserves rigorous control over state and rules while allowing compatible engines to share a single renderer. New environments can thus be authored by coding agents from text or image inputs, then edited and extended entirely in code without creating bespoke visual assets for every scene.AgentGartencode worlds1

Operating a video model as an interactive neural renderer requires it to strictly follow updated engine conditions, maintain visual consistency across extended rollouts, and synthesize observations in fine-grained, short blocks so that agents receive immediate feedback after brief actions. We adapt a pretrained bidirectional video model to structured conditions, convert it to block-causal generation, and distill it into a real-time renderer on a single GPU with , which trains the renderer on its own rollouts via distribution matching and introduces two key advances. First, to allow later losses to update the history-encoding computation without the memory cost of a fully differentiable rollout, we adopt two-pass training and introduce : a block-by-block execution schedule that eliminates numerical divergence between sampling and recomputation and achieves bitwise-identical recomputation of the rollout trajectory. Second, to prevent the visual degradation that score distillation alone exhibits over long rollouts, we incorporate a real-data adversarial objective and derive an exact R1/R2 regularization scheme for a discriminator with a frozen backbone, entirely avoiding double-backward passes through fused attention kernels.Adversarial Forcing[, , ]8910[]11exact replay[, ]1012

Code worlds provide rich environments for agents to practice and evolve. We evaluate pretrained foundation-model agents across rounds of interaction, where they perceive the world strictly through rendered observations, diagnose failures, and distill key insights into written inherited by subsequent rounds. In hide-and-seek , agents rapidly grounded abstract spatial knowledge into closed-loop physical execution, with ramp use and shelter construction emerging within a handful of games. The same reflective loop improved performance across rounds in several additional, diverse environments (Section ).playbooks[]135

A framework for code worlds that couples persistent, editable environment state to a shared real-time neural renderer through structured conditions, enabling programmable interaction and diverse visual observations across compatible engines without per-scene visual asset authoring.

, a distillation method for a few-step, block-causal neural renderer. 2.1

A code world combines a scene program $p$ , an engine that executes it, and a neural renderer $R_{\theta}$ . The program specifies the scene and interaction rules. Let $s_{t}$ denote the scene state, including object poses, articulations, and task variables; $\pi_{t}$ the observing camera pose; and $a_{t}$ the actions of one or more agents. The engine updates the state and captures a structured condition $c_{t}$ from the camera:

$(s_{t+1},\pi_{t+1})=f_{p}(s_{t},\pi_{t},a_{t}),\qquad c_{t}=h_{p}(s_{t},\pi_{t}),$ (1)

where $f_{p}$ implements the state transition and $h_{p}$ renders the visible geometry. Given an appearance reference $x_{0}$ and a text description $y$ , the neural renderer generates subsequent observations from visual history $x_{ $x_{t}=R_{\theta}\!\left(x_{(2)

The agent receives $x_{t}$ and selects $a_{t}$ , which determines the next state and condition through Eq. ().1

Unlike a video world model, whose state resides in generated history, the transition $f_{p}$ takes no rendered observation as input: the renderer influences the state only through the actions that agents select, so rendering errors cannot accumulate in the state. A recorded state trajectory can consequently be rendered again under a different appearance reference or camera without altering the underlying events. Conversely, the renderer observes the state only through $c_{\leq t}$ ; attributes that the conditions leave undetermined, such as color and material, are specified by $x_{0}$ and $y$ and carried by the visual history. The renderer consumes conditions and visual history in blocks, as described in Section .3

2.2

We use colorized depth or surface normals as structured conditions. Both can be estimated from video or rendered by an engine, and their three-channel representation allows us to reuse the pretrained video encoder and Transformer. For real videos, we obtain depth with ViPE , using Depth Anything 3  as its depth backend, and normals with NormalCrafter . Simulated scenes supply these maps directly from geometry, without requiring detailed materials or textures. During training, each sample uses one randomly chosen modality (Section ).[]14[]15[]163.2

We encode depth with the Vision Banana mapping  and camera-space unit normals as $(n+1)/2$ , using consistent coordinate and orientation conventions across estimated and rendered maps (Appendix ).[]17A.2

2.3

A coding agent constructs a code world from either a single image or a text description, producing an executable scene program along with an appearance reference $x_{0}$ . Because appearance is delegated to the neural renderer, the scene program does not require detailed materials or leaf-level assets; it only needs coarse geometry that faithfully conveys layout, silhouettes, occlusion, and motion dynamics.

From an image.

The input image serves simultaneously as $x_{0}$ and the reference layout (Figure ). Perception and generation models lift the visible content into instance masks , monocular depth and camera intrinsics , 3D bounding boxes , and extracted object meshes . A coding agent fits these assets to the estimated geometry, completes unobserved regions as plausible spatial extensions, and binds physical properties and interaction rules.2[]18[]15[]19[]20

From text and agentic refinement.

When building from text, the agent writes the scene program directly using geometric primitives and engine assets. An initial render is transformed into $x_{0}$ via an image editing model while preserving scene layout. In both modalities, the agent refines the scene through an interactive feedback loop: it evaluates test rollouts from multiple probe cameras, inspects engine verification queries (contact, collision clearance, and occlusion), and iteratively repairs faulty poses, unsupported structures, or ambiguous motions before deployment.

We train a geometry-conditioned autoregressive video model to implement the renderer in Section . Starting from a pretrained bidirectional backbone, training proceeds through geometry conditioning, teacher-forcing adaptation, and . The final stage combines distribution matching on the model’s own rollouts with exact history-gradient replay and real-data adversarial training. A bounded key–value cache and streaming decoding support continuous inference within the interaction loop in Figure .2.1Adversarial Forcing1

3.1

We initialize from Cosmos 3-Nano and separate its understanding (UND) and generation (GEN) towers. The frozen UND tower encodes the caption $y$ into per-layer keys and values consumed by GEN. This separation allows independent compilation and distributed execution of the two towers; during distillation, the student, teacher, and fake-score networks share one UND tower and reuse its outputs for the same caption.[]21

A frozen Wan video autoencoder maps RGB and geometry videos to latents. The appearance reference $x_{0}$ uses the backbone’s native clean-frame representation: it receives no diffusion timestep and is never denoised. Architecture sizes and training configurations are given in Appendix .[]22A.1

3.2

Condition tokens.

Depth and normals use the three-channel encodings of Section . Spatial average pooling reduces the condition encoder’s input size and the number of tokens processed during training and inference. For an encoded condition frame indexed by $t$ , we form2.2

$G_{t}=W_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathcal{P}\!\big([E(S(c))]_{t}\big)+e_{\mathrm{geo}},$ (3)

where $S$ pools the condition video spatially, $E$ is the frozen video encoder, and $\mathcal{P}$ groups latent patches. We reuse the pretrained RGB input projection $W_{\mathrm{in}}$ and add a zero-initialized modality embedding $e_{\mathrm{geo}}$ . Condition tokens receive no diffusion timestep.

Joint attention.

We concatenate geometry and RGB tokens along the sequence dimension and process them with the same Transformer layers. We use neither channel concatenation nor control branches , to avoid imposing a pixel-aligned inductive bias. Writing $R_{t}$ for RGB latent tokens, the visual sequence is[]23[, ]2425

$[\,G_{0},G_{1},\dots\,]\;[\,R_{0},R_{1},\dots\,],$ (4)

with $R_{0}$ encoding $x_{0}$ and text keys and values integrated via cross-attention. Geometry and RGB share temporal rotary coordinates; spatial coordinates map both grids to the same image extent. This preserves geometric alignment while allowing cross-token interactions. Only noisy RGB tokens produce velocity predictions.

Robust conditions.

Geometry estimated from natural video differs from engine-rendered geometry in texture leakage, alignment, and missing observations. To reduce dependence on estimator-specific cues, we randomly retain depth or normals, with occasional dropout of both modalities; dropped inputs are black. We suppress fine texture by down- and upsampling, perturb alignment with a smooth spatial warp anchored to the first frame, and add noise to condition latents. Preprocessing and augmentation settings appear in Appendix .A.2

Stage 2 adapts the geometry-conditioned model to blockwise autoregressive generation. We partition the latents after the reference into fixed-length blocks. Each block is generated from its aligned geometry and previously completed blocks, without access to future blocks.
