    4.1

    We evaluate four representative triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering methods, covering different designs in geometry connectivity, opacity, and appearance (Tabs.  and ):Methods.12

  • •

    replaces Gaussian primitives with independent planar triangle facelets and renders them through differentiable alpha blending. Its opacity function is defined using barycentric coordinates, with a compactness parameter controlling the transition from diffuse splats toward sharper triangle surfaces.2DTS()Sheng et al., 2025

  • •

    directly optimizes independent triangles using a differentiable window function confined to each projected triangle. Learned opacity, view-dependent color, and depth-ordered alpha blending support image-based optimization, while adaptive densification and pruning refine the allocation of triangles.Triangle-Splatting()Held et al., 2026b

  • •

    represents scenes with a compact triangle soup carrying neural texture features and binary opacity. Stochastic opacity masking makes binary opacity trainable within a depth-tested rasterization pipeline, while a neural color decoder maps texture features to rendered colors.DiffSoup()Tojo et al., 2026

  • •

    constructs a shared-vertex mesh through restricted Delaunay triangulation and jointly refines geometry and per-vertex spherical-harmonic appearance. Opacity and window parameter schedules progressively guide optimization toward opaque triangles.MeshSplatting()Held et al., 2026a

    • The first three methods produce without explicit shared-vertex connectivity, whereas MeshSplatting produces an . We audit the structure of its exported mesh in Sec. . We additionally include 3DGS and 2DGS as Gaussian-based reference baselines.triangle soupsindexed mesh4.4()Kerbl et al., 2023()Huang et al., 2024

    We evaluate on four complementary datasets spanning real-world environments and object-centric captures:Datasets.

  • •

    comprises nine real scenes, with surrounding camera trajectories, cluttered geometry, and large depth variations that challenge reconstruction of both foreground and distant content.Mip-NeRF 360()Barron et al., 2022

  • •

    For , we use the two outdoor scenes and , featuring large real-world objects, complex backgrounds, and occlusions.Tanks and Temples()Knapitsch et al., 2017traintruck

  • •

    provides laboratory captures of varied objects from 49 or 64 calibrated camera positions per scene, together with structured-light reference scans, enabling geometric evaluation alongside image fidelity.DTU()Jensen et al., 2014

  • •

    contains eight object-centric scenes with detailed geometry and realistic non-Lambertian materials, complementary to real captures.NeRF-Synthetic()Mildenhall et al., 2020

    • We follow the original training pipelines while applying the shared data and evaluation protocols. Images are downsampled according to each method’s requirements. All training and evaluation use a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU with 24 GB memory.Implementation details.

    End-to-end FPS includes CPU processing and GPU rendering. We also report GPU median (P50) and 95th-percentile (P95) frame latency, together with renderer graphics allocations.Timing and resource measurements.

    Before comparing methods, we check our reproductions against published results and public codebases. Across all 27 Mip-NeRF 360 method–scene pairs with published per-scene results, the mean absolute PSNR difference is only 0.075 dB and the maximum relative deviation is below 0.8%. Fig.  shows this close agreement in image quality. Appendix Tab.  provides dataset-level comparisons against paper values and public-code results.Reproducibility.37

    Tab.  reports the standardized Source Renderer results across all four datasets. On Mip-NeRF 360 , NeRF-Synthetic , and DTU , 2DTS achieves the highest PSNR (28.16 dB, 33.65 dB, and 29.66 dB), while using the least peak training memory on NeRF-Synthetic and DTU (3172 MiB and 2470 MiB). Triangle-Splatting achieves the lowest LPIPS on Tanks and Temples (0.171) and DTU (0.080). DiffSoup renders and trains fastest on three datasets (up to 371 FPS and 12.2 $\sim$ 16.8 min), but has lower image quality (18.90 dB on Tanks and Temples). MeshSplatting uses shared-vertex connectivity and trains fastest on DTU (10.7 min), with lower PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360 (24.72 dB). Thus, representation dominates fidelity, throughput, memory, and training time simultaneously.3()Barron et al., 2022()Mildenhall et al., 2020()Jensen et al., 2014no

    DTU complements NVS metrics with surface accuracy against reference scans (Tab. ). Results show that image quality and surface accuracy do not always yield the same ranking. While 2DTS leads in both PSNR (29.66 dB) and CD (0.63 mm), Triangle-Splatting achieves the lowest LPIPS (0.080) with a higher CD of 1.27 mm. MeshSplatting has similar PSNR to Triangle-Splatting (27.82 vs. 27.78 dB) but lower surface error (0.80 mm CD), while DiffSoup has the highest CD (3.89 mm). These results motivate evaluating image quality and surface geometry jointly before graphics deployment.2D novel-view fidelity vs. 3D surface geometry.3

    Tab.  compares quality and throughput across the three settings on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples; Appendix Fig.  summarizes the PSNR trajectories of the four triangle- and mesh-based methods.     The evaluated triangle- and mesh-based methods rely on specialized appearance models or compositing operations that limit their direct compatibility with conventional opaque mesh pipelines. Our Standard Mesh Deployment tests this compatibility using static vertex colors and hardware Z-buffering. Methods that depend on rendering operations beyond this pipeline can lose substantial image quality when adapted to it.Deployment quality.

    On Mip-NeRF 360, adapting 2DTS, Triangle-Splatting, and MeshSplatting to Standard Mesh Deployment lowers mean PSNR by 15.64 dB, 12.36 dB, and 4.89 dB, respectively, relative to the Source Renderer (Tab. ). MeshSplatting has the smallest overall deployment gap ( $\Delta Q_{m}^{\mathrm{deploy}}$ ) among these three methods. The rendered examples illustrate the visual losses: 2DTS produces large opaque shards on , and Triangle-Splatting exhibits a similar failure on (Fig. ).4bonsaitreehill4

On Mip-NeRF 360, these implementations recover 2.69 $\sim$ 10.76 dB PSNR over Standard Mesh Deployment across 2DTS, Triangle-Splatting, and MeshSplatting, corresponding to their portability gaps ( $\Delta Q_{m}^{\mathrm{port}}$ ). They still fall short of the Source Renderer: the remaining adaptation losses ( $\Delta Q_{m}^{\mathrm{adapt}}$ ) are 4.88 dB for 2DTS, 4.17 dB for Triangle-Splatting, and 2.20 dB for MeshSplatting. Appendix Fig.  shows these changes across the three settings.7

    4.4

    We audit MeshSplatting’s exported indexed meshes across all four datasets using the three metric groups defined in Sec. . Tab.  reports the mean of each metric over all scenes in each dataset. We consider the large, unbounded scenes of Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples separately from the smaller, object-centric scenes of DTU and NeRF-Synthetic. Appendix Sec.  provides per-scene results and audit details. We highlight the following results:3.46C

  • •

    Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples exhibit similar vertex sharing, with mean $|\mathbf{V}|/|\mathbf{F}|$ ratios of 0.523 and 0.516 and mean valence of 6.49 on both datasets. The object-centric datasets show greater reuse: DTU and NeRF-Synthetic have lower $|\mathbf{V}|/|\mathbf{F}|$ ratios of 0.428 and 0.339, with higher valence of 7.36 and 8.59, respectively. Vertex sharing is evident in both scene groups, but its extent differs.Local reuse.

  • •

    Vertex sharing does not ensure manifoldness. On Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples, approximately 18% of edges and 65 $\sim$ 66% of vertices are non-manifold. On DTU and NeRF-Synthetic, the non-manifold-edge ratios rise to 22% and 28%, and the non-manifold-vertex ratios to 73% and 87%, respectively. Thus, greater reuse on the object-centric datasets coexists with more non-manifold neighborhoods. Boundary edges account for 37 $\sim$ 46% of edges across the four datasets, indicating open surfaces while such boundaries can be expected in partially observed scenes. Non-manifold edges and vertices, in contrast, violate local manifold connectivity, and lower ratios indicate better local structural integrity.Local structure.

  • •

    On the large-scene datasets, the largest connected component (LCC) contains approximately 70% of faces, with 69% of surface area on Mip-NeRF 360 and 67% on Tanks and Temples. On DTU and NeRF-Synthetic, the LCC contains 77% and 80% of faces and 78% and 80% of area, respectively. Despite these dominant components, approximately 20 $\sim$ 30% of faces and 20 $\sim$ 33% of area remain distributed across other components. Together with mean component counts in the tens to hundreds of thousands, these fractions reveal substantial fragmentation in both scene groups. Absolute component counts depend on mesh size and do not provide a structural-quality ranking across datasets. On the two deployment datasets, MeshSplatting’s leading Standard Mesh Deployment image quality among the four studied methods (Tab. ) coexists with these structural defects, showing that visual fidelity does not ensure structural integrity.Global connectivity.4

    • 5

    We introduced MeshSuite, a unified benchmark for triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering that connects evaluation with official Source Renderers to graphics-engine deployment. MeshSuite combines standardized evaluation protocols, a unified asset interface, and method-specific Unity renderers to compare the Source Renderer, Standard Mesh Deployment, and Custom Engine Deployment. It evaluates visual fidelity and computational cost alongside surface accuracy and mesh structural integrity. Our experiments show that visual quality and method rankings depend on the deployment setting. Custom Engine Deployment better preserves appearance but incurs higher runtime costs than Standard Mesh Deployment. Among the four studied methods, mesh splatting methods achieve the highest image quality under Standard Mesh Deployment on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples, yet their exported meshes exhibit non-manifold structures and substantial fragmentation across both large, unbounded and object-centric scenes. These findings show that triangle rasterization and shared-vertex connectivity alone do not ensure practical graphics usability. Evaluation must jointly consider appearance preservation, rendering efficiency, and the structural requirements of downstream tasks. Future work can extend the benchmark to additional graphics engines and directly assess exported meshes in tasks such as editing, remeshing, and collision handling.

    • Appendix A

    Fig.  details the modular software architecture of , expanding the conceptual overview in Fig. . The infrastructure is built with decoupling and modularity as first principles, ensuring that model training, format translation, graphics-engine deployment, and multi-dimensional evaluation operate independently through clearly specified interfaces.6MeshSuite1

    MeshSuite is organized into five cohesive subsystems: (1) : Standardizes canonical camera frames, optical axes, field-of-view definitions, and resolution downsampling across datasets. For masked object captures (, DTU), this layer automatically computes object alpha mattes and applies the white-background compositing convention specified in Eq. . (2) : Provides standardized training harnesses wrapping the official implementations of 2DTS , Triangle-Splatting , MeshSplatting , and DiffSoup . It follows each method’s original training pipeline while applying shared data and evaluation protocols under a common single-GPU hardware environment. (3) : The central translation bridge implementing method-specific adapters $\mathcal{E}_{m}$ . It parses trained model parameters and extracts explicit geometry, opacity fields, and appearance representations into standardized intermediate assets $\mathcal{A}_{m}$ . (4) : In-engine renderers implemented in Unity using C# Scriptable Render Pipelines and custom HLSL shaders. This layer provides both Standard Mesh Deployment and Custom Engine Deployment. (5) : Automated evaluation scripts computing standard 2D image fidelity metrics (, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS), hardware timing profiles (GPU P50/P95 latency percentiles and memory allocations), and geometric mesh topology audits.Modular Component Design.Dataset Managemente.g.1Algorithm Pool and Training()Sheng et al., 2025()Held et al., 2026b()Held et al., 2026a()Tojo et al., 2026Universal Translation LayerGraphics Engine DeploymentEvaluation and Audit Suitee.g.

    Under the Universal Translation Layer, trained models are converted into portable asset files prior to engine execution. Independent triangle soup models (2DTS, Triangle-Splatting, DiffSoup) are serialized into flat vertex arrays and attribute textures, whereas indexed meshes (MeshSplatting) are serialized with shared vertex coordinate tables, triangle face indices, and per-vertex SH coefficients. Crucially, the resulting asset bundles are completely self-contained and ingested directly by the graphics engine, decoupling real-time deployment from PyTorch, CUDA extension compilers, and Python runtime overhead. This architectural separation allows new neural rendering representations to be benchmarked by implementing a single translation adapter, and enables future deployment to other graphics engines (, Unreal Engine, Blender) without modifying upstream training pipelines.Asset Serialization and Decoupled Execution.e.g.

    Appendix B

    Tab.  complements the per-scene PSNR reproduction differences illustrated in Fig.  with comprehensive dataset-level evaluations comparing our reproduced metrics against published paper numbers and official public repositories. Sec.  outlines the primary experimental setup.734.1

    For 2DTS, Triangle-Splatting, and MeshSplatting, MeshSuite closely matches published dataset-level PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples. On Mip-NeRF 360, the mean absolute PSNR difference across their 27 scene-method pairs is only 0.075 dB, and the maximum relative deviation across these pairs is below 0.8%. Specifically, 2DTS reproduces at 28.16 dB PSNR (vs. 28.18 dB in the paper and 28.51 dB in the public repository), Triangle-Splatting achieves 27.13 dB (vs. 27.17 dB reported and 27.20 dB in public code), and MeshSplatting achieves 24.72 dB (vs. 24.78 dB in both paper and code). For DiffSoup, where per-scene Mip-NeRF 360 results were not reported in the original paper, MeshSuite is closer to the public codebase in dataset-level PSNR (23.54 dB vs. 23.69 dB) than to the paper (24.76 dB); on Tanks and Temples, it achieves 18.90 dB vs. 18.38 dB in public code. LPIPS differences are larger for several methods, so close PSNR agreement does not imply equal agreement across all image metrics.Quantitative Reproduction Fidelity.1 DiffSoup is omitted since it does not report per-scene metrics in its original paper.11

    Differences between published figures, public repositories, and MeshSuite may reflect preprocessing, camera conventions, background compositing, metric implementations, and numerical variation. We do not isolate their individual contributions: (1) : Image interpolation filters can affect reconstructed image values; MeshSuite applies shared data preparation while retaining the downsampling requirements of each method (Sec. ). (2) : Differences in principal point handling and coordinate conventions can affect alignment; MeshSuite enforces standardized projection matrices aligned with graphics conventions. (3) : On masked datasets such as DTU, prior works alternated between evaluating against unmasked black backgrounds and masked white backgrounds; MeshSuite standardizes all evaluations to the alpha matte white-background protocol (Eq. ). (4) : MeshSuite uses a common metric implementation, including VGG-based LPIPS (Sec. ), while parallel floating-point accumulation can also introduce numerical variation. The comparisons document agreement and remaining differences rather than establishing a single cause for them.Sources of Discrepancies and Impact of Standardization.Image Downsampling Kernels4.1Camera Intrinsics and Principal PointsBackground Compositing Conventions1Metric Implementations and Numerical Variation3.1

    D.1

    Fig.  visualizes the PSNR trajectories of the four studied triangle- and mesh-based NVS representations across the Source Renderer, Standard Mesh Deployment, and Custom Engine Deployment on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples. Tab.  summarizes the corresponding GPU latency percentiles (P50 and P95) and active graphics memory allocations, providing an extensive dataset-level view that expands the compact summary in main-text Tab. .7105

    Across both deployment benchmarks, the visual quality trajectories reveal a consistent two-tier pattern: (1) : Unconstrained triangle soup methods (2DTS and Triangle-Splatting) rely heavily on soft blending kernels and continuous opacity to represent fine structures and semi-transparent boundaries. When forced into Standard Mesh Deployment—where triangles are treated as fully opaque surfaces with hardware Z-buffering—these methods suffer dataset-mean PSNR drops of 11.02 $\sim$ 15.64 dB relative to the Source Renderer. In scenes with complex foliage or fine geometric thinness (, or ), overlapping transparent triangles collapse into severe opaque, jagged polygon shards (see Fig. ). (2) : In contrast, MeshSplatting exhibits far greater resilience under Standard Mesh Deployment, dropping by only 4.89 dB on Mip-NeRF 360 (19.83 dB vs. 24.72 dB) and 6.15 dB on Tanks and Temples (14.38 dB vs. 20.53 dB). Because its geometry is constrained to an indexed mesh surface, disabling alpha compositing causes significantly fewer occluding artifacts, allowing it to lead the four triangle- and mesh-based methods under Standard Mesh Deployment despite lower initial Source Renderer fidelity.Cross-Setting Trajectory Analysis.Severe Deployment Degradation for Triangle Soupse.g.treehillbonsai4Surface-Constrained Resilience in MeshSplatting

    As reported in Tab. , Custom Engine Deployment preserves image quality at the expense of substantial computational and memory overhead. On Mip-NeRF 360, Custom Engine Deployment increases GPU P50 latency by approximately 5.8 $\sim$ 7.6 $\times$ compared to Standard Mesh Deployment, based on the displayed dataset means (2.1 $\sim$ 6.4 ms vs. 0.3 $\sim$ 1.1 ms), while mean renderer graphics allocations for these three methods increase from 54 MiB to 927 $\sim$ 1559 MiB. DiffSoup represents a distinct operating point: utilizing neural texture decoding rather than millions of independent Gaussian-like primitives, it achieves sub-millisecond GPU latency (0.4 $\sim$ 0.5 ms) and mean renderer graphics allocations of 276 $\sim$ 288 MiB, though at the cost of lower overall image fidelity (17.02 $\sim$ 23.15 dB).Runtime Resource Trade-Offs.10

(3) : Incorporating geometric priors during training is vital to penalize non-manifold edges and fragmentation for downstream physics.Engine Deployment Recommendations.Standard PipelinesHigh-Framerate XRTopological Regularization

    Appendix E

    Fig.  illustrates the qualitative rendering behavior of 2DGS on the scene across the evaluated deployment protocols, serving as a supplement to the triangle- and mesh-based methods in Fig. .8()Huang et al., 2024counter4

    In Sec. , 2DGS and DiffSoup illustrate opposing extremes of graphics-engine compatibility. DiffSoup couples explicit triangle geometry with neural feature textures: while its neural color decoder prevents native execution under the fixed-function Standard Mesh Deployment protocol, our custom engine shader successfully preserves its appearance under Custom Engine Deployment (reaching 23.15 dB on Mip-NeRF 360 and 18.90 dB on Tanks and Temples). In contrast, 2DGS operates as a collection of 2D oriented planar Gaussian splats rendered with a specialized tile-based splatting rasterizer. To extract polygonal geometry, 2DGS integrates truncated signed distance field (TSDF) fusion across depth maps predicted by the splats, exporting an explicit indexed triangle mesh with per-vertex colors. However, this meshing process completely discards the underlying 2D Gaussian covariances, normal vectors, and view-dependent opacity blending models. Consequently, 2DGS is fundamentally incompatible with our Custom Engine Deployment pipeline (marked in Fig.  and Tab. ), as the exported asset retains no splatting primitives for in-engine custom rasterization.Asymmetry with Neural Feature Decoding.4.3N/A84

    While the reconstructed TSDF mesh can be natively imported and rasterized via standard graphics pipelines at high frame rates (exceeding 4000 FPS on Tanks and Temples and 2700 FPS on Mip-NeRF 360), relying strictly on an opaque triangle surface with static vertex coloring induces drastic perceptual fidelity degradation: (1) : On the metallic mixing bowl shown in Fig. , the official Source Renderer accurately captures sharp, specular reflections and metallic sheen (27.02 dB dataset-mean PSNR). Under Standard Mesh Deployment, the shiny surface collapses into diffuse, cloudy shading, completely erasing the specular highlight in the highlighted red inset. (2) : As shown in the cyan inset (cutting board and background plastic containers), fine object boundaries and high-frequency textural details are blurred out during TSDF voxel discretization and marching cubes extraction. The lack of alpha transparency around thin structures causes occluded background elements to either disappear or merge unnaturally with foreground objects. (3) : Across Mip-NeRF 360, this geometric transition causes a 14.65 dB drop in dataset-mean PSNR (from 26.79 dB to 12.70 dB) and increases LPIPS from 0.252 to 0.594 (Tab. ). These qualitative artifacts confirm that standard triangle mesh conversion cannot faithfully preserve the appearance of 2D Gaussian primitives without specialized real-time engine shaders.Visual Degradation under Standard Mesh Deployment.Loss of View-Dependent Reflection8Geometric Oversmoothing and Boundary ArtifactsQuantitative Contrast4

item.description:

License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.11430v1 [cs.GR] 10 Sep 2026

Gaussian Light Transport

2717SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers; December 01–04, 2026; Kuala Lumpur, MalaysiaConference: SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers (SA Conference Papers ’26), December 01–04, 2026, Kuala Lumpur, MalaysiaDOI: 10.1145/3829340.3842373979-8-4007-2842-6/2026/12ISBN: Computing methodologies Ray tracingCCS: Patrick Attimont email: patrick.attimont@inria.fr, , Affiliation: INRIA - Grenoble UniversityGrenobleFrance, Kartic Subr email: K.Subr@ed.ac.uk, , Affiliation: University of EdinburghEdinburghUnited Kingdom and Cyril Soler , , Affiliation: INRIA - Grenoble UniversityGrenobleFranceemail: cyril.soler@inria.fr© cc

Abstract.

We present a novel method for computing global illumination by expressing the solution to the light transport equation as a 13D Gaussian mixture model over positions, directions, surface normals, and material properties. We show that including scene properties in the Gaussian representation drastically reduces the number of functions and speeds up evaluation. As opposed to traditional light transport methods based on Neumann series, the parameters of our model are directly estimated by minimizing the residual of the rendering equation. While both optimization and rendering require repeated evaluations of a linear combination of high-dimensional Gaussian functions, we introduce an efficient culling strategy to keep the optimization tractable and produce renderings in real time. Our representation enables to render fast, view-independent solutions to the light transport equation, achieving rendering times on the order of milliseconds, with a fraction of the memory requirements of conventional neural rendering approaches.

Global illumination, Gaussian mixtures

Keywords:

†by†cc-license:

1.

Efficient computation of global illumination in 3D environments is a long-standing problem in computer graphics. Solving the integral equation —which models the equilibrium of directional radiant light energy—would yield a radiance field which can be used to render photo-realistic images from any viewpoint. This remains an elusive goal, due to the recursive nature of the equation which unravels as infinite-dimensional integrals. In this paper, we represent the solution to the equation as a sum of Gaussians and optimize the parameters of the Gaussians to approximately satisfy the equation.()Kajiya, 1986

Previous approaches have uncovered trade-offs between by solving the global radiance field vis-a-vis view-dependent solutions. Galerkin methods (such as radiosity ) yield global solutions but are impractical for representing high-frequency effects due to reflections, caustics, shadows, etc. On the other hand, naive path tracing  tends to require heavy computation for smooth effects due to global illumination. The approach for contemporary light transport solutions is Monte Carlo integration of the Neumann series expansion of the rendering equation, yielding a general and effective solution. View-dependent methods require recomputation for novel views within a scene, but are usually justified when there are dynamic elements. We propose a method for view-independent rendering that is effective for multi-view rendering (e.g. fly-throughs) of complex, static scenes. In other words, “view-independent” means that the calculation is not tied to the parameters of a camera (as path tracing would), and computes the entire light field that solves the transport equation. View-dependent images are thereafter produced by slicing this light field for a given camera.View-Independent Rendering()Goral et al., 1984()Kajiya, 1986de facto

Several methods from machine learning have been adapted for rendering . Image-based rendering approaches such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)  and Gaussian Splatting  aim to hypothesize arbitrary views given multi-view images as input. Neural radiosity optimizes a neural field, defined on a discrete grid, to minimize the residual of the rendering equation .()Keller et al., 2018()Mildenhall et al., 2020()Kerbl et al., 2023(; )Hadadan et al., 2021Su et al., 2024

We propose a new view-independent method for solving the light transport equation by leveraging the versatile and adaptive nature of Gaussian kernels. We represent the solution to the light transport equation as the sum of 13D Gaussians over the full spaces of positions, directions, normals, and material properties, and optimize these parameters to minimize the residual of the light transport equation. Our Gaussian kernels are therefore not restricted to remain on surfaces and inherently handle local variations in normals and materials. This allows us to compute a view-independent approximation to the solution to the rendering equation at a fraction of the memory cost of neural methods. We exploit the local support of Gaussians to design a culling strategy for a fast evaluation of the model, enabling efficient optimization (in a matter of minutes) and real-time rendering (see Figure ). In summary,2

  • •

    we propose a novel approach to solving the light transport equation by directly optimizing Gaussians, to obtain a view-independent solution;

  • •

    the complexity of our model adapts to the solution and is not constrained by the geometry of the scene;

  • •

    we show that this approach matches or improves on existing neural methods in quality, while training $10$ – $23$ $\times$ faster and rendering $2$ – $4$ $\times$ faster, with a memory footprint of just a few megabytes.

    • 2.

    2.1.

    Galerkin radiosity  and directional finite element methods  project solutions onto structured basis functions defined over the scene geometry. They involve solving a linear system and provide view-independent solutions with theoretical guarantees. However, the need to parameterize geometry and directions makes them poorly suited to complex scenes with intricate geometry or highly glossy materials. Representing radiance as a 5D function leads to a prohibitive memory cost for fine basis functions that are required to capture phenomena such as caustics and glossy reflections. Collocation methods, including meshless formulations , alleviate some discretization constraints but do not fundamentally resolve these scalability issues.Galerkin and Collocation Methods.(; )Goral et al., 1984Zatz, 1993()Heckbert and Winget, 1991(; ; )Lehtinen et al., 2008Christensen, 2008Wang et al., 2015

    Monte Carlo methods avoid explicit function representations by estimating the solution through stochastic sampling, typically via a Neumann series expansion of the rendering equation. Path tracing and its extensions—including bidirectional path tracing , photon mapping , and Metropolis Light Transport —are highly effective at handling complex light transport phenomena. They are flexible, but can exhibit noise from high variance when long light paths are involved, making them computationally expensive and poorly suited to view-independent global illumination. Path re-using methods , temporal reprojection  and gradient-domain path tracing  mitigate this problem by making the best of already computed sub-parts of the light transport for new views in their own specific ways.Monte Carlo and Path Tracing Methods.()Veach, 1997(; )Jensen, 1996Hachisuka et al., 2008()Veach and Guibas, 1997()Ouyang et al., 2021()Schied et al., 2017()Kettunen et al., 2015

    One other limitation of path tracing methods is their inherent ignorance of the spatial and angular bandwidth of the reconstructed signal, causing high variance in low frequency parts of the image. Frequency-aware splatting  and adaptive low-frequency methods  partially address these issues.()Belcour et al., 2013()Jarosz et al., 2011

    2.2.

    Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) methods compute light transport matrices that allow scene elements such as view points and light , scene geometry  and materials  to be changed interactively when rendering novel views. More recently, combine precomputed radiance transport with 3D Gaussian splatting to interactively generate images with indirect illumination—as opposed to global illumination. PRT methods struggle to locally adapt to the radiance field, leading to heavy memory requirements. This is further exacerbated by the basis functions (wavelets, spherical harmonics, etc.) being tied to the geometry.PRT and Radiance caching.(; )Sloan et al., 2023Ng et al., 2004()Iwasaki et al., 2007()Sun et al., 2007Guo et al. (2024)

    Radiance caching (and irradiance caching)  accelerates global illumination for non-Lambertian scenes by precomputed storage of radiance in a world-space grid. This can be stored on surfaces  or in a volumetric grid . Novel views are rendered by simply convolving the BRDFs with incoming radiance from the cache. Storage requirements of these methods are high (gigabytes) but rendering can be an order of magnitude faster (10 ms) than PRT. These methods make use of their precomputed cache to retrieve indirect illumination only, while our evaluated radiance fields include both direct and indirect illumination as a proxy.()Křivánek et al., 2008()Tatzgern et al., 2024()Xing et al., 2024

    Several approaches trade physical rigor for efficiency and compactness. Data-driven bases  model the space of solutions using learned low-dimensional representations, enabling efficient relighting. Point-based and volumetric approaches such as point-based radiance fields , Plenoxels , and Gaussian splatting  optimize for visual metrics. Neural radiance fields (NeRF)  learn continuous volumetric representations of radiance from images and render novel views via ray integration. Recent methods use 3D Gaussian Splatting for radiance caching , and Gaussian mixtures for path guiding . fit rendered light fields with Gaussians, conditioned on G-Buffers, using geometry, material, and normalized scene-variable information to efficiently model high-quality, view- and scene-dependent appearance. These approaches have triggered numerous extensions including for dynamic scenes . While highly effective for view synthesis, these methods typically approximate observed radiance distributions (i.e. pre-acquired or pre-rendered data) and are not physically based nor solve the rendering equation.Alternative representations.()Belcour et al., 2022()Zhang et al., 2023()Yu et al., 2021()Kerbl et al., 2023()Mildenhall et al., 2020()Bauer et al., 2026()Vorba et al., 2019Diolatzis et al. (2024)()Coomans et al., 2024

    Neural radiosity  represents radiance using a neural network trained to minimize the residual of the rendering equation over a dense grid of points that is unaware of the frequency content of the represented light field. Its extension to dynamic scenes has also been proposed . A key limitation of these approaches is their lack of adaptivity to scene content, resulting in a large memory footprint due to uniform discretizations (e.g., 5D grids). Recent work mitigates this issue by attaching neural representations to the scene geometry , improving efficiency but still tying the representation to the underlying mesh and material properties, or by using multiresolution hash encoding .Neural Approaches.()Hadadan et al., 2021()Su et al., 2024()Su et al., 2025()Müller et al., 2022

    3.

    Our goal is to optimize a radiance field to solve the rendering equation in a synthetic scene. The equilibrium of light transport in a scene is governed by the rendering equation ()Kajiya, 1986

    (1) $\displaystyle L(\mathbf{x},\omega)=E(\mathbf{x},\omega)+\int_{\Omega}L_{i}(\mathbf{x},\omega^{\prime})f(\mathbf{x},\omega,\omega^{\prime})\mathbf{n}\cdot\omega^{\prime}d\omega^{\prime},$

    where $\Omega$ is the upper hemisphere of directions, $L_{i}(\mathbf{x},\omega^{\prime})$ is the incident radiance at $\mathbf{x}$ along $\omega^{\prime}$ , $f$ is the reflectance function, $\mathbf{n}$ is the normal at $\mathbf{x}$ , and $E$ is emitted radiance. In operator form, with the linear light transport operator $\mathbf{T}$ , this equation is :()Arvo, 1995

    (2) $\displaystyle L=E+\mathbf{T}L.$

    We seek to solve Equation  with a parameterized radiance function $\theta\mapsto L_{\theta}$ with $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , by minimizing its residual:2

    $\theta^{*}=\mbox{argmin}_{\theta}\|r_{\theta}\|^{2}\mbox{~~~~~~~\;\;with\;\;~~~~~~~}r_{\theta}=L_{\theta}-E-\mathbf{T}L_{\theta}.$

    In contrast to the Neural Radiosity framework that represents $L$ using a neural network , we use an explicit sum of localized Gaussian kernels, which allows adapting the location and number of functions to the spatial and angular frequency content of the solution $L_{\theta^{*}}$ leading to lower memory requirements.()Hadadan et al., 2021

    Our training objective is the squared $L_{2}$ norm of the residual of the rendering equation over the surface area and angular domains:

    (3) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta)$ $\displaystyle=\|r_{\theta}\|^{2}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\int_{\Omega}r_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\omega)^{2}\;d\omega d\mathbf{x}.$

    We compute $L_{\theta}$ by combining a classical optimization loop with additional steps to optimize the number of kernels—and therefore the memory cost—of our representation of the actual solution to equation . The remainder of this section describes our function space and optimization procedure.2

    We represent $L_{\theta}$ as a weighted sum of $M$ (variable) $13$ D-Gaussians over position $\mathbf{x}$ , direction $\omega$ , normal $\mathbf{n}$ , material attributes (albedo $a$ and roughness $r$ ):Parameterized radiance space.

    (4) $L_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^{M}c_{k}e^{-(\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{m}_{k})^{\intercal}\Sigma_{k}^{-1}(\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{m}_{k})},$

    where $\mathbf{q}=(\mathbf{x},\omega,\mathbf{n},a,r)\in\mathbb{R}^{13}$ , $\mathbf{m}_{k}$ and $\Sigma_{k}$ are the mean and covariance matrix of the $k$ Gaussian and $c_{k}$ is its radiance scaling coefficient. While albedo and positions are naturally 3D, normals and directions are plunged in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , and roughness is unidimensional. This approach, similar to the one of , enables sharing Gaussian contributions between nearby points in the scene even when the points do not belong to one contiguous region. For instance, surfaces with spatially-varying materials could share a Gaussian across regions of identical albedo and roughness. See Section  for a discussion on replacing $\Sigma$ with a block-diagonal matrix. Note that this set of variables does not limit the range of materials that can be used in a scene, but simply facilitates a better adaptation of the Gaussians to variations in the illumination. We initialize using 10K Gaussians centered at randomly sampled surface points and directions, with low-intensity colors before optimization.thDiolatzis et al. (2024)4

    The loss in Equation  is estimated using Monte Carlo integration and gradients of the loss with respect to $\theta$ are estimated using stochastic gradient descent. Surface points $\mathbf{x}_{j}$ , outgoing (resp. incoming) directions $\omega_{j}$ (resp. $\omega^{\prime}_{j}$ ) are generated following adapted probability density functions $p(\mathbf{x},\omega)$ . The gradients of the loss are thereby estimated as:Gradient estimation.3

    (5) $\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{2r_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{j},\omega_{j})\nabla_{\theta}r_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{j},\omega_{j})}{p(\mathbf{x}_{j},\omega_{j})}.$

    Ideally, unbiased gradient estimates would require the inner integrals in $r_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{j},\omega_{j})$ and $\nabla_{\theta}r_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{j},\omega_{j})$ to be evaluated using independent samples. Following the semi-gradient formulation of Cho and Cho , we instead drop the gradient of the inner integral entirely, backpropagating only through $r_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{j},\omega_{j})$ , trading a small amount of bias for a significant reduction in gradient variance.()2024

    We adapt the density of Gaussians where the residual is large, improving the efficiency of the Gaussian mixture $L_{\theta}$ via splitting/spawning and pruning steps.Densification and pruning.

    We split Gaussians that exhibit large gradients within specific subspaces since this indicates under-resolved variations . We split them along the principal axis of the corresponding subspace. While splitting refines the existing structure, it cannot introduce primitives in regions with no coverage. Thus we additionally perform residual-driven spawning: while computing the residual $r(\mathbf{x}_{j},\omega_{j})$ in Equation , we select the top- $k$ samples with the highest contribution, and initialize new Gaussians centered at the corresponding locations $\mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x}_{j},\omega_{j})$ . Their initial radiance coefficient $c_{k}$ is set proportional to the estimated scattered radiance at these samples given by the right-hand side of the residual $c_{k}=E(\mathbf{x},\omega)+\mathbf{T}L_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\omega)$ , which naturally estimates $L_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\omega)$ for subsequent optimization.()Kerbl et al., 20233

    We prune Gaussians based on their relative normalized contributions, $r_{k}$ for each Gaussian $G_{k}$ , w.r.t. the global radiance field $L_{\theta}$ . We restrict the integration domain to the effective support $\mathcal{D}_{k}$ of each Gaussian, i.e. the region of $\mathcal{S}\times\Omega$ where the exponent of $G_{k}$ exceeds a minimum value $\beta=-14$ :

    (6) $r_{k}=\int_{\mathcal{D}_{k}}\frac{c_{k}G_{k}(\mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x},\omega)-\mathbf{m}_{k})}{L_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\omega)}\,d\mathbf{x}\,d\omega.$

    We estimate this integral via the Monte-Carlo estimator

    (7) $r_{k}\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{c_{k}G_{k}(\mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x}_{j},\omega_{j})-\mathbf{m}_{k})}{L_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{j},\omega_{j})}.$

    Gaussian kernels whose contribution $r_{k}$ falls below a threshold $\tau$ are considered negligible and are removed from the representation. We use $\tau=8\times 10^{-3}$ for all experiments. Thus, we prune based on relative energy contribution rather than absolute magnitude, allowing both bright and low-intensity regions to be treated consistently.

    3.1.

    We produce images from the learned model using two alternative ways: (1) which simply evaluates $L_{\theta}$ for every visible point $\mathbf{x}$ in the scene along directions $\omega$ pointing toward the camera; or (2) , where one bounce of rays are traced from the camera and the right-hand side of Equation  is evaluated by integrating the incident illumination $L_{i}$ at this point using $L_{i}(\mathbf{x},\omega^{\prime})=L_{\theta}(\mathbf{y},\omega^{\prime\prime})$ denoting $(\mathbf{y},\omega^{\prime\prime})$ as the coordinates of the point seen from $\mathbf{x}$ in direction $\omega^{\prime}$ .GSGS + MC1

    Both optimization and rendering queries necessitate the evaluation of contributions from potentially large numbers of Gaussian kernels. While queries generated during rendering exhibit strong spatial and directional coherence, this is not the case during training or when rendering with , where samples are drawn randomly over both position and direction, which precludes screen-space tiling strategies, such as those used in .GSGS + MCKerbl et al. (2023)

    For efficient evaluation of $L_{\theta}$ , we introduce a simple yet effective world space tile-based culling strategy that drastically reduces the number of Gaussian functions to evaluate per query. Each query is assigned a 64-bit Morton code based on the index of the shape it lies on and its 3D position. Queries are then sorted according to their Morton codes and grouped into tiles by truncating the code to a fixed prefix length. This grouping ensures spatial locality while improving memory coherence during evaluation. For each tile, we compute conservative bounding ranges across all $13$ input dimensions. These bounds are obtained via parallel reductions over the queries assigned to each tile and are used to perform Gaussian/tile intersection tests to cull irrelevant primitives. If the expected exponent falls below a predefined threshold, the Gaussian contribution to the tile is considered negligible and is discarded, effectively truncating each kernel to a finite region of support. This hierarchical culling strategy drastically reduces the number of Gaussian kernel evaluations per query. Typically on the scene this strategy allows us to only evaluate 76 Gaussian kernels on average per pixel, among a total of 22K.Bedroom

    4.

    We implemented our optimization and rendering steps within the Mitsuba / Python framework, which provides easy management of scenes and lighting primitives . The Gaussian representation and training pipeline are implemented using PyTorch. To achieve high efficiency during both training and inference, model evaluation and analytic derivative computations are implemented through custom Taichi kernels .()Jakob et al., 2022()Hu et al., 2019

    In the naïve version of our algorithm, covariance matrices are represented using their Cholesky decomposition $\Sigma=\mathbf{L}^{\intercal}\mathbf{L}$ , where $\mathbf{L}$ is a lower $13\times 13$ triangular matrix. With this choice we haveCovariance matrices.

    $\mathbf{v}^{\intercal}\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{v}=\|\mathbf{L}^{-1}\mathbf{v}\|^{2},$

    which means that computing each Gaussian term in Equation  boils down to solving a single $13$ D triangular linear system. We found that an interesting trade-off is to turn the full 13-dimensional Gaussian representations into a product of lower-dimensional Gaussians, thereby neglecting the possible correlation between some of the dimensions. Each Gaussian $G_{k}$ is modeled as a product of independent Gaussians over these subspaces. Although this factorization limits the ability to capture cross-subspace correlations, we find that it has a relatively low impact on the quality of the converged models, while significantly improving performance by maintaining spatial locality in 3D. In all results shown in this paper, position, direction, material and normals are treated as separate subspaces. Following , the covariance matrices of the position and direction components are decomposed into a scaling matrix $\mathbf{S}$ and a rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$ :4Kerbl et al. (2023)

    $\Sigma=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}^{\intercal}\mathbf{R}^{\intercal},$

    making the evaluation of $\mathbf{v}^{\intercal}\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{v}$ even faster.

    Gaussian colors and covariance scales both use an exponential activation, since radiance and scale values lie in the range $[0,\infty)$ .

    Because radiance is optimized in linear space, applying the naïve loss function of Equation  would prioritize learning bright regions at the expense of darker ones. To mitigate this, we found very effective to normalize the loss by the current prediction of the model:Loss function.3

    (8) $\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\left\|\frac{r_{\theta}}{\nabla_{0}(L_{\theta})+\epsilon}\right\|^{2},$

    where $\nabla_{0}(L_{\theta})$ is in effect $L_{\theta}$ , but considered constant when differentiating.

    Additionally, we observed that regions containing near-coincident surfaces—such as object contact areas or thin geometric interfaces—present sharp discontinuities that the optimization tries to resolve by strongly elongating the Gaussian kernels along their positional components. We mitigate this by introducing an anisotropy penalty term $\mathcal{P}(\theta)$ in the loss function for the three positional components. Let $\mathbf{s}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ denote the logarithmic scaling parameters of Gaussian $i$ , with components $\mathbf{s}_{i}=(s_{i,1},s_{i,2},s_{i,3})$ . We define the mean logarithmic scale as

    (9) $\bar{s}_{i}=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{n=1}^{3}s_{i,n}.$

    The anisotropy regularization term is defined over all Gaussians as

    (10) $\mathcal{P}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{ReLU}\left(\sum_{n=1}^{3}(s_{i,n}-\bar{s}_{i})^{2}-\epsilon\right),$

    where $\epsilon$ controls the tolerated level of anisotropy. In our implementation, we use $\epsilon=2.5$ . Figure  illustrates the visual improvement brought by this anisotropy regularization term.4

    In summary, the full expression of the loss function we are using during the optimization step is

    $\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\left\|\frac{r_{\theta}}{\nabla_{0}(L_{\theta})+\epsilon}\right\|^{2}+\lambda_{\mathrm{aniso}}\mathcal{P}(\theta),$

    where $\lambda_{\mathrm{aniso}}$ monitors the compromise between the shape of the Gaussian in position and the resulting fit of Equation . We used $\lambda_{\mathrm{aniso}}=0.008$ in all our examples.1

    During the estimate of gradients (Equation ) we sample $Q$ incident directions and $Q$ explicit light samples in $r_{\theta}$ for each outgoing direction $\omega_{j}$ , so as to reduce variance due to the generally significant contribution of direct illumination. In all our examples, we used $Q=32$ .Optimization.5

    Since the evaluation of $r_{\theta}$ requires $L_{\theta}$ to be computed twice, we concatenate the queries of both evaluations into a single tensor that is evaluated once, making the economy of one spatial reordering and culling per iteration. Additionally, culling is reused during the backward pass to speed up backpropagation.

    During the Gaussian splitting phase, each candidate Gaussian is split along a single subspace at a time with priority given to spatial dimensions, in order to ensure that the child Gaussians accurately approximate their parent, and to preserve continuity during optimization. The child Gaussians are initialized by offsetting them in opposite directions along the principal axis of the parent, at a distance $d=0.5$ times the principal scale, and scaling their covariance by a factor $k=0.8$ along this axis.

    We use the Adam optimizer . All runs use the same hyperparameters, and learning rates for ( $\mathbf{m}$ , $\mathbf{R}$ , $\mathbf{S}$ , $c$ ) are set to ( $3\times 10^{-4}$ , $1\times 10^{-3}$ , $5\times 10^{-3}$ , $1\times 10^{-2}$ ). Gaussians are split every 400 iterations, and 500 new Gaussians are spawned every 500 iterations. Both splitting and spawning stop at iteration 15000. Gaussians are pruned every 2000 iterations throughout training.()Kingma and Ba, 2015

    We exploit the separability of our Gaussian functions to derive an efficient separable culling criterion. Specifically, we evaluate a Mahalanobis distance between the Gaussian and the tile bounds independently in each subspace. Because the Gaussian exponent decomposes additively across decorrelated subspaces, these per-subspace distances can be accumulated to form a global bound. We first apply this test to the 1D subspaces, which provides a cheap and effective early rejection mechanism, then a similar test is performed for the 3D spatial and directional components using the tile’s bounding box. For 3D subspaces, a good conservative Mahalanobis distance between a tile bounding box and a Gaussian can be computed as follows: we first compute the Mahalanobis distance from the Gaussian to the center of the bounding box, from which we subtract the maximum distance from the center of the bounding box to one of its corners. Similarly to Hadadan et al. , the model does not directly learn light distributions over perfectly specular surfaces. Instead, during both rendering and optimization, paths are extended until the first smooth surface.Rendering.()2021

    5.

    Our representation shares similarities with N-dimensional Gaussians : by centering Gaussians on scene features (albedo, normals), high-frequency content is encoded directly in the input space rather than learned. Their method fits pre-generated path-traced images, solving transport beforehand, whereas we solve the rendering equation itself. We keep fewer principal component axes than their full representation (see Section ). Dropping this generality allows us to derive a more efficient culling strategy well suited for real-time rendering, while reducing the memory footprint of our representation.()Diolatzis et al., 20244

    Our method belongs to the larger family of kernel-based approximations. For instance, our adaptive Gaussian mixture is equivalent to constructing a Gaussian process with a location-dependent covariance function, i.e. a nonstationary kernel where the notion of distance changes across space. Similarly, neural network approximations (e.g. Neural Radiosity ) implicitly define a kernel, but use fixed positions on a predefined grid. As a comparison, our model not only learns kernel weights but also positions $\mathbf{m}_{k}$ in $13$ D, shape (covariance matrices $\Sigma_{k}$ ) and number of nodes to use. Finally, our model can also be understood as a learned radial basis function neural network, that implicitly constructs a nonstationary Gaussian process kernel. In different domains Gaussian processes and kernel methods have been applied to solve partial differential equations , while sparsity-promoting techniques improve efficiency .()Hadadan et al., 2021(; )Chen et al., 2021Xu et al., 2025()Vakili et al., 2022

    One advantage of our adaptive representation is that it avoids the pitfalls of bandwidth-limited constructions .()Soler et al., 2022

    Since $L_{\theta}$ appears twice in the expression of the residual $r_{\theta}$ , the model must be evaluated twice: for outgoing radiance, and at the intersection points for incident radiance. This can be interpreted numerically as a recursive training approach, where the model iteratively uses its own previous state as the best estimate so far to the solution of the rendering equation.

    The calculation of $r_{\theta}$ is currently conducted using uniform sampling of surfaces, which favors the learning of Gaussians with a large positional footprint. We noticed that glossy reflections on curved surfaces are learned quicker with a sampling that is based on curvature. We think that sampling according to a local prediction of angular and spatial bandwidth  would eventually focus the workload on regions that need it.Limitations.()Belcour et al., 2013

    Our current implementation runs on static scenes only. We think that if single objects are moved or scene parameters such as reflectance properties or lighting are changed, it would be highly beneficial to start from the previous solution and continue optimizing from there. Another possible avenue for predefined changes would be to add an extra temporal dimension to Gaussian functions.

    Our culling approach relies on the assumption that queries grouped within a tile are coherent both spatially and angularly. While this assumption holds well for primary camera rays during rendering, it becomes weaker during training and rendering, where queries exhibit reduced spatio-directional correlation. Consequently, directional culling becomes less effective, resulting in a 1.5 $\times$ inference slowdown in the worst case. Future work could investigate direction-aware tiling or clustering schemes to better preserve spatio-directional locality under these workloads.GSGS + MC

    Like any Gaussian-based representation, ours is smooth by construction and resolves a discontinuity only where an input announces it. Albedo, normal and roughness jump at material and geometric edges, so boundaries aligned with them stay sharp (Fig. ). Position and direction vary continuously, so radiance discontinuous in those alone is interpolated and softened. Near-specular reflections show it most: the chimney’s dark base in , and the bright highlight along the seat edge in (Fig. ).6Living RoomChair8

For each viewpoint we show the rendered vs. flattened Gaussians, the directional component of which makes their visualized support ellipsoids move along with the camera.1

Although the limited total number of Gaussians used to represent the solution inherently biases the result, visual and LIP comparisons with the path traced reference prove very satisfactory.5F()Andersson et al., 2021F

Gaussian components naturally decompose into diffuse + glossy components when BSDFs contain multiple lobes.8

    7.

    We presented a novel method for solving the rendering equation based on a mixture of Gaussian functions, which allows real-time exploration of the solution to the problem of global illumination in static scenes. The very low memory footprint of our representation makes it easy to embed in a viewer for instance to explore architectural constructions.

    Our plans for future work include extending our method to the integro-differential equation for global illumination in participating media, and the export of light fields. The intrinsic local support of our representation in frequency space also naturally allows to isolate/scale/cancel parts of the solution to the light transport equation by their corresponding spatial and angular frequency. This could for instance be used to box-filter the signal as a post-process for artistic reasons. More generally our model could be used for baking global illumination thanks to its very economic memory footprint.
