RenderFormer-V2: Neural Rendering with Heterogeneous Scene Primitives

Chong ZengStanford University, USA Affiliation: Yue DongMicrosoft Research, China Affiliation: Pieter PeersCollege of William & Mary, USA Affiliation: Lvmin ZhangStanford University, USA Affiliation: Maneesh AgrawalaStanford University, USA Affiliation: 

Abstract

We present ’RenderFormer-V2’, a unified learned transformer-based neural rendering model, complementary to modern physics-based rendering systems, that can handle diverse light-transport effects such as caustics, volumetric scattering, environment lighting, textured and displaced surfaces and out-of-distribution materials without per-scene training or specialized code. RenderFormer-V2 models global light transport as a sequence-to-sequence transformation. Following its predecessor, RenderFormer-V2 also employs a two stage process: a view-independent stage that resolves intra-scene primitive to primitive transport, and a view-dependent stage that transforms the internal neural scene representation into image pixels. Different from RenderFormer, our model employs a novel combined windowed-attention and rendering-informed attention sink in the view-independent stage to improve scalability while maintaining render accuracy. To further improve versatility, RenderFormer-V2 supports heterogeneous scene primitives, including environment maps and participating media, and it employs a material encoding independent of the underlying surface reflectance model that encodes material appearance via a novel neural embedding. We demonstrate the versatility of RenderFormer-V2 on a variety of scenes and perform an extensive ablation of the improved attention mechanism.

Neural Rendering, Transformer, Neural Material Embedding, Windowed Attention, Attention Sink

Keywords:

1

Neural rendering aims to visualize virtual scenes without relying on manually encoded rules of light transport, but instead based on relations between geometry, materials, and light learned from data. Many neural rendering solutions offer limited generalizability beyond the training data  or rely on per-scene training strategies . Recently, RenderFormer  formulated light transport simulation as a regressive sequence-to-sequence translation problem, where an input sequence of triangle tokens is transformed into pixel-patch tokens through a transformer-based two stage pipeline: a view-independent stage that resolves light transport between triangles, and a view-dependent stage that resolves transport from triangles to the camera. Once trained, RenderFormer can render a wide variety of virtual scenes without fine-tuning or further training. Although RenderFormer is more general than prior solutions, it is still far from practical: it is limited to scenes of less than $4$ k triangles, it only supports a hard-coded GGX BRDF model , and it is limited to scenes with (max. $8$ ) triangular diffuse light sources.[, ]1211[]30[]43[]33

In this paper we introduce ’RenderFormer-V2’, a versatile transformer-based neural rendering system that addresses RenderFormer’s limitations via a number of carefully designed architectural innovations (). Similar to RenderFormer, RenderFormer-V2 formulates light transport simulation as a regressive sequence-to-sequence translation. RenderFormer’s main bottleneck in supporting larger triangle meshes is the brute-force self-attention between triangle tokens in the view-independent stage. Not only does this have a quadratic complexity with respect to the number of triangles, it also leads RenderFormer to loose focus for very large triangle meshes. Inspired by recent advances in supporting larger context windows for large-language models, RenderFormer-V2 employs a novel sparse-attention variant, consisting of a combination of windowed attention  and render-aware attention-sinks , tuned for resolving view-independent light transport. Furthermore, to improve generalizability, we allow for other primitives than triangles (e.g., voxels) and employ a simpler positional encoding based on the centroid of the primitive.Figure 1[]21[]37

RenderFormer-V2 further decouples the material specification from a hard-coded BRDF model, and instead employs a latent material embedding for encoding different BRDF models including transparent and measured materials. A key observation is that the latent material encoding does not need to be invertible to the input (BRDF) parameters, but it only needs to encode the appearance of the material; we rely on RenderFormer-V2 to learn how to map the material appearance into pixel values. Moreover, to model spatially varying materials, we reuse a pretrained VAE encoder  to encode $32\times 32$ texture patches (of latent material properties) per primitive. Similar to the latent material appearance space, we only require the VAE encoder, and let RenderFormer-V2 learn how to interpret the encoded textures during rendering.[]35

Whereas RenderFormer has a dedicated emittance parameter associated with each triangle to model light sources, we leverage RenderFormer-V2’s ability to mix different primitives to embed different lighting types, ranging from triangular light sources to environment maps, into specialized tokens.

We demonstrate the versatility of RenderFormer-V2 by rendering more complex and larger scenes than RenderFormer with a greater variety in lighting and materials. We perform an in-depth ablation study to validate our design decisions. The trained RenderFormer-V2 model and code can be found at: .https://renderformer.github.io/v2

2

Neural Rendering

aims to predict the effects of light transport through a virtual scene. Early work in neural rendering employs specially learned neural representations of the scene  and thus are overfitted to a single or limited number of scenes. To circumvent the need to learn neural scene representations, image-space neural rendering systems  take as input G-buffers of intrinsic components of the scene, and output a shaded image seen from the same viewpoint. Because the G-buffers only capture a portion of the scene, image-space neural rendering methods must necessarily hallucinate (or ignore) transport between visible and non-visible parts of the scene.[]30[, , , , ]1112421448[, , ]204424

Recently, a new class of neural rendering systems leverage attention layers  to model light transport between 3D primitives. Xu et al.  model diffuse light transport in a point cloud representation of the scene. Closest to our method is RenderFormer  which employs a two-stage transformer architecture that models the transport: (1) between triangles and (2) from the triangles to the camera. However, RenderFormer employs a brute-force attention mechanism which does not scale well to large triangle meshes. Moreover, RenderFormer only supports triangles as geometric primitives, diffuse (triangle-shaped) light sources, and a per-triangle hard-coded GGX microfacet BRDF model . In contrast, RenderFormer-V2 employs an efficient sparse attention mechanism to support a large number ( $>100$ k) of primitives, and flexible geometry, lighting, and materials representations and textures.[]31[]38[]43[]33

Long Context Modeling with Transformers

Classic transformers compute attention between all pair-wise token combinations, resulting a quadratic complexity with respect to the number of tokens in the sequence. Moreover, when the sequence grows, attention per-token tends to decrease and be spread over many tokens, and as a consequence the transformer loses focus, resulting in a decreased performance. Addressing both issues is critical for scaling a transformer-based rendering architecture beyond a few thousand tokens. Here, we focus on the most relevant classes of transformer scaling methods, and refer to Tay et al.  for a detailed overview.[]29

Windowed attention mechanisms  focus on addressing the compute complexity, and built on the observation that in many cases proximity is a good indicator of importance, and hence these mechanism hard-constrain the attention computation to a small window around the target token. Consequently, windowed attention mechanisms ignore long-range interactions which can be important for light transport modeling. More generally, windowed attention mechanisms belong to a class of attention methods that employ static attention patterns  and their effectiveness is highly dependent on whether the attention sparsity matches the attention pattern. While light transport through a scene can be sparse, it does not follow a pre-determined sparsity pattern.[, , , ]2140363sparse[, , ]192516

Native-Sparse Attention (NSA)  dynamically determines the sparseness by employing three different attention streams: (i) a sliding window to capture local attention, (ii) compressed attention that determines the importance of groups of input tokens, and (iii) a fine-grained attention on the groups of tokens identified as important. However, the computational cost of NSA is significantly higher than static sparse attention patterns due to the secondary retrieval stage. Moreover, NSA requires Grouped-Query Attention  which lowers the model’s capacity, and thus adversely affects performance.[]41[]1

Hierarchical attention mechanisms (e.g., ) leverage the observation that attention tends to be focused near the query, and that the attention variation at distant tokens decreases. Hence, by creating a multi-resolution hierarchy of token and computing attention with the token selected from the hierarchy based on distance, attention can be better focused and more efficiently computed. However, multi-resolution hierarchies implicitly assume that positional distance is proportional to distance in the sequence or image, and thus implicitly assume a (regular) uniform spatial distribution of tokens. This is not the case for 3D scenes, where primitives are clustered at various points in space (i.e., objects). Point Transformer v3  addresses this limitation by (i) serializing the point cloud along space-filling curves, and (ii) grouping and padding to ensure the point cloud is divisible by the target patch size. While, Point Transformer v3 improves speed and memory overhead, its implementation is more complex and is computationally more expensive than sparse attention methods. We employ a less complex and resource intensive strategy for extending the context window using a similar serialization strategy as Point Transformer v3.[, , ]395045[]36

Xiao et al.  observed that the soft-max operation in the attention computation tends to excess attention in a single token (i.e., attention sink). A similar behavior was also observed in vision transformers . To avoid attention being dumped in a random token, Xiao et al.  propose to keep a few dedicated attention sink tokens to model global relations and a local sliding windowed attention to model local relations. This local-global dichotomy has been further refined in follow up work . We also build on this idea, and introduce rendering-relevant semantics for the sinks. First, we place all light sources in the sinks as these are likely to interact with all surfaces. Second, inspired by the compressed tokens in NSA , we add to the sink summarization tokens for groups of primitives based on Hilbert space-filling curves.[]37’dump’[]18[]37[, ]4723[]41

3

RenderFormer-V2 builds and improves on RenderFormer . We therefore first review RenderFormer’s architecture before detailing RenderFormer-V2.[]43

RenderFormer is an end-to-end trained transformer-based neural renderer that takes as input a sequence of triangles with GGX BRDF parameters  and emittance strength, as well as camera parameters, and it outputs a rendered image of the scene with full global illumination. RenderFormer consist of two stages with a slightly different architecture. The first (i.e., view-independent) stage, consisting of $12$ self-attention layers , transforms the input sequence of embedded triangle tokens (expressed in coordinates) to a sequence of per-triangle tokens which encode triangle-to-triangle light transport. The second stage (i.e., view-dependent stage), consisting of 6 repetitions of a cross-attention layer  followed by a self-attention layer, operates on view-bundle tokens. A view-bundle token is an embedding of a $8\times 8$ grid of camera rays expressed in the coordinate system. The cross-attention layer computes the attention between the view-bundle tokens and the transformed triangle tokens from the first stage. The view-dependent stage is followed by a dense vision transformer to convert the transformed ray-bundle tokens into pixel values for each ray. The triangles are embedded as the sum of: (a) the per-vertex normal embedding (using NeRF positional encoding with 6 frequencies that is subsequently expanded to the $768$ token-length vector through a linear layer), (b) the GGX BRDF parameters (expanded by a linear layer to the $768$ token-length vector), and (c) the monochrome emittance (expanded by a linear layer). RenderFormer adapts RoPE  to apply a relative positional encoding on the $9$ D vector obtained by stacking the $3$ D coordinates of the triangle’s vertices. RoPE is applied at each layer in RenderFormer with the vertices expressed in world coordinates in the view-independent stage and in camera coordinates in the view-dependent stage. Hence, only the ray direction of the $8\times 8$ camera rays is embedded by stacking the $64$ view rays and subsequently expanded them to a $768$ length ray-bundle embedding via a linear layer. RenderFormer is trained end-to-end, first at a $256\times 256$ resolution and with scenes containing at most $1.5$ k triangles followed by a second training stage where the output resolution is increased to $512\times 512$ and the triangle count is increased to $4$ k. RenderFormer is trained with a weighted $L_{1}$ and LPIPS  loss on log-transformed reference renders.[]33[]31world[]31camera[]27[]46

4

Similar to RenderFormer, RenderFormer-V2 features a two-stage transformer-based neural rendering pipeline where the first stage resolves view-independent intra-primitive transport and the second stage transforms view-dependent ray-bundles to output tokens based on the transformed scene primitives from the first stage. However, RenderFormer-V2 deviates from RenderFormer is a number of critical steps: (i) RenderFormer-V2 is not limited to only triangle tokens and it supports a mixture of different scene primitives, including different types of light sources (), and (ii) RenderFormer-V2 scales better in terms of efficiency and accuracy to a larger number of scene primitives (). summarizes the RenderFormer-V2 pipeline.Section 5Section 6Figure 2

5

We represent a virtual scene as a sequence of heterogeneous tokens that encode geometry, material, lighting, and camera information. In contrast to RenderFormer where the positional encoding is tailored to triangles as scene primitives, and which relies on a hard-coded camera-transformation to encode the camera position, we employ a uniform relative positional encoding strategy for all tokens (including ray-bundles):

  • 1.

    For (e.g., geometric primitive or camera) we use RoPE to encode the centroid of the concept with a RoPE dimension of $40$ (i.e., 20 frequencies). RoPE ensures that the scene embedding is invariant to scene translations.tokens representing a concept with a 3D spatial location

  • 2.

    For (e.g., environment map) we employ RoPE using the centroid of the whole scene to ensure that translating the scene does not affect the relative attention computation between tokens from both categories.tokens representing positionless concepts

    • As the different concepts are defined by different parameters, we employ a separate embedding for each token type, and rely on the training process to enable RenderFormer-V2 to differentiate between the different primitive embeddings.

    5.1

    To embed a triangle, we first embed the different components (vertices, normals, and materials) and combine them via addition into the final token.

    Vertex Embedding

    We stack the 3 positions of vertices (minus the centroid of the triangle) in a $9$ D vector, and apply (NeRF) positional encoding  with $12$ frequencies exponentially spaced between $2^{0}$ and $2^{11}$ . Finally, we apply a (trainable) linear layer to expand to a token-length (i.e., $768$ ) vector followed by RMS-normalization.[]22

    Normal Embedding

    We apply the same process as for vertex embedding to encode the per-vertex normals. Note, the vertex and normal embedding use separately trainable linear layers for expansion.

    Material Embedding

    We desire an embedding of material appearance that is not tied to a particular BRDF model. Inspired by prior work on learning a latent embedding for BRDFs , we also learn a material appearance embedding. A key advantage of RenderFormer-V2’s transformer architecture is that it is powerful enough to directly learn how to evaluate the embedded material appearance (given the view and lighting) without the need to rely on a pretrained reverse mapping from latent code to material appearance. As we are interested in encoding the appearance rather than the exact BRDF, we follow an encoding inspired by Serrano et al.’s  perceptual material similarity metric and embed rendered images of a sphere under the Uffizi Gallery light probe. We opt for a sphere for it simplicity and the Uffizi Gallery light probe because it is color neural and it contains a good mix of low and high frequency lighting features . Practically, we employ a CNN-based auto-encoder with a $9$ D latent feature vector at the bottleneck. We pretrain this encoder with an L1 loss on images rendered with Blender Cycles of randomly generated materials with the Principled BRDF model . Furthermore, to encourage a coherent manifold, we apply a smoothness regularization term , and a $\tanh$ activation to constrain the values in the embedding to $[-1,+1]$ . visualizes the learned latent material appearance space. While we currently use the Principled BRDF model for generating training data, this can easily be extended to include other analytical BRDF models or measured BRDFs. For efficiency, we also train an additional MLP for each analytical BRDF model (after the latent space is trained) to map its parameters directly into the latent space to bypass the need to render a sphere; for measured BRDFs we render the material and use the pretrained encoder.[, , , , , ]281749131026[]26[]4[]5[]9Figure 3

    Texture Embedding

    To support spatially varying materials, we embed all materials in a texture. For each triangle, we first project the BRDF parameters into the learned latent space and subsequently rasterize the per-triangle texture ( $9$ channels), local normal map ( $3$ channels), and a displacement map (as a $1$ channel height offset) in $32\times 32$ image patches, which we subsequently encode with a pretrained VAE  into an $4\times 4$ $80$ -channel latent feature map. Finally, we compress the feature map via a single learnable linear layer to a $768$ -length vector and add it to the token embedding.[]35

    5.2

    To demonstrate RenderFormer-V2’s ability to handle heterogenous geometric primitives, we also encode voxels filled with a scattering medium into a separate token-type.

    Rotation and Scale Embedding

    For each voxel we encode the rotation matrix and scale vector that describes the voxel’s relative rotation and per-axis scale in world coordinates. Similar to the normal encoding for triangles, we employ (NeRF) positional encoding with $12$ frequencies, which is subsequently expanded via a linear layer to a token-length vector.

    Scattering and Absorption

    As (RGB) scattering and (RGB) absorption coefficients are optical parameters of scattering media, and thus model independent, we opt to directly encode them. In addition, we also encode the anisotropy coefficient of the scattering function, yielding a $7$ D vector. To support spatially-varying scattering, we encode a $4\times 4\times 4$ volumetric texture of the $7$ D scattering feature vector, and linearly project the feature vector into a token-length vector that is added to the rotation and scale embedding.

    5.3

    Similar to RenderFormer, we embed triangular light sources with homogeneous diffuse emittance. In contrast to RenderFormer, we store colored RGB emittance as an explicit light source token (instead of combining it with geometry tokens) which is expanded via a separate linear layer to the token-length. Similar to the triangle primitives, we add the vertex positions and per-vertex normals embedding to the token.

    5.4

    We follow an environment encoding similar to DiffusionRenderer .[]20

    Texture Embedding

    We store both an LDR (clamped to $[0,1]$ ) and (log-encoded) HDR version (normalized by the log maximum value) of the environment map at $512\times 256$ resolution, and encode each map using a pretrained VAE  yielding a $64\times 32\times 16$ latent feature map for each. This feature map is too large to store in a single token. Hence, we opt to split the latent feature map in $8\times 4$ patches (of size $8\times 8\times 16$ ) that are compressed by a linear layer into two token-length vectors; hence yielding separate LDR and HDR environment map tokens.[]35

    Direction Embedding

    While a environment map token does not have a position, each pixel in the $64\times 64$ pixel patch does correspond to a lighting direction. To make RenderFormer-V2 aware of the exact bundle of rays that correspond to the pixels in the patch per token, we create a direction map that, for each pixel, stores the corresponding (normalized) 3D direction vector in world coordinates. This direction map is projected via a linear layer to a token-length vector and added to the environment lighting embedding.

    Lighting Strength Embedding

    During texture embedding we normalized the log-encoded HDR by the log maximum value. To retain this information, we expand this value to a token-length vector and add it to the final embedding.

    5.5

    Similar to RenderFormer, we embed the (normalized) ray directions in an $8\times 8$ map, and project it to a token-length vector using a single linear layer. Whereas in RenderFormer the ray directions are expressed in camera coordinates, we encode them directly in world coordinates; the origin of the ray bundle is already taken care of via the uniform relative positional encoding strategy.

    6

    While RenderFormer-V2 follows RenderFormer’s two stage design, each stage differs in how attention is computed. We first discuss the modification to the second stage (i.e., view-dependent), follow by the more significant modifications to the first stage (i.e., view-independent).

    6.1

    Unlike RenderFormer’s view-dependent stage, RenderFormer-V2’s view-dependent stage operates in world coordinates (rather than camera coordinates). Moreover, we replace the full self-attention layers by SWIN windowed attention layers  with a window size of $8$ and a shift of $4$ . While the computation cost changes modestly from $\mathcal{O}(T\times R+R^{2})$ to $\mathcal{O}(T\times R+W^{2})$ ( $T$ is the number of scene tokens (the dominating factor), $R$ the number of ray-bundles, and $W$ the window size), its main advantage is the ability to scale to larger resolutions more easily because the context window size is now resolution independent.[]21

    6.2

    The view-independent stage is the main bottle neck when increasing the number of tokens as computation cost scales quadratically with the number of primitives. Moreover, when the sequence grows large, naive attention tends to loose focus, resulting in a loss of render fidelity. While often the dominating factor, primitive-to-primitive light transport is not solely a local phenomena; a subset of global factors such as illumination and large-scale occlusion can significantly affect light transport through the scene. Hence, we combine attention from local primitives with attention from global tokens, while mitigating focus-loss on large sequences.

    Sorting & Serialization

    Unlike ray-bundles, scene primitives are not regularly spaced, making it more challenging to exploit locality while retaining efficient GPU-computation. Inspired by Point Transformer v3 , we sort and linearize geometry tokens using Hilbert curves such that nearby (in the 1D sequence) tokens are likely close in 3D space too. This allows us to model local attention with sliding window attention ; we take $256$ tokens before and after the target token, yielding a computational complexity independent of the number of primitives.[]36[]3

    Attention Sinks for Rendering

    To model global light transport, we adapt attention sinks . The tokens in the attention sink are always included in the attention calculations. We strategically assign three different token types with rendering relevant semantics to the sink:[]37

  • 1.

    : we add $16$ register tokens  to the input sequence for storing storing global information.Global Register Tokens[]6

  • 2.

    : it is likely that the light transport on most geometric primitives is directly affected by the light sources in the scene. Hence, by placing the light sources in the sink we ensure that each light source is taken in account for each primitive regardless of distance. Conceptually, the attention computation with respect to the light sources is analogous to importance sampling the light sources in path tracing.Light Source Tokens

  • 3.

    : while long range light transport is important, we argue that the precise details of distant geometry matter less. Therefore, we model long-range interactions with a coarser geometry representation. Specifically, we perform mean pooling over every $64$ consecutive geometry tokens to form a summarization token that we add to the attention sink.Summarization Tokens

    • 7

    Training Data

    Similarly to RenderFormer, we generate scenes by placing $1$ to $3$ randomly selected objects from the ObjaVerse dataset in one of four randomly selected template scenes (a ground plane with one, two or three walls). Different from RenderFormer’s scene generation process, we assign randomly generated materials (using the Principled BRDF model  mapped into our material appearance latent) from the following five categories: (a) homogeneous opaque diffuse+specular material ( $2/9$ chance; with the sum of the diffuse and specular albedo restricted to $[0.9,1]$ , and roughness log-sampled in $[0.01,1]$ ), (b) a homogeneous opaque material with metallic+roughness parameters ( $2/9$ ), (c) a diffuse+specular SVBRDF randomly sampled from the MatSynth SVBRDF dataset  ( $1/9$ ), (d) a metallic+roughness SVBRDF from MatSynth ( $1/9$ ), or (e) a homogeneous transparent metallic+roughness material ( $3/9$ ; with metallic sampled in $[0,1]$ , roughness log-sampled in $[0.01,1]$ , and each RGB channel of the base color sampled in $[0,1]$ ). In $2/3$ of the scenes, we add one (1/2) or two (1/2) volumes with randomly chosen scattering and absorption. The camera is randomly placed and aimed at the scene with a FOV chosen between $30^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$ . Unlike RenderFormer, we allow the camera to be placed inside the scene. Up to $8$ triangular light sources are randomly placed outside the scene with a random (RGB) intensity between $2,\!500$ and $5,\!000$ $W/m^{2}$ . Furthermore, for $5/6$ of the scenes, we add environment lighting randomly selected from PolyHaven. To avoid color bias, we randomly swap the color channels in the environment map. Each scene is rendered offline using Blender Cycles with $4,\!096$ samples per pixel. For efficiency, we pre-generate a training dataset of $\sim\!10$ M randomly sampled scenes spanning resolutions $256^{2}$ – $2048^{2}$ with $1$ k– $64$ k primitives, totaling $\sim\!70$ TB.[]5[]32

    Loss Function

    We employ the same loss as RenderFormer:

    $L_{1}(\log I)+0.05\ L_{LPIPS}(clamp(\log I/\log 2,0,1)),$ (1)

    where the log encoding of the image $I$ serves to avoid specular reflections dominating the L1 error, and the LPIPS loss  minimizes perceptual differences.[]46

    Training Process & Refinement

    We employ a five-stage training regime to first focus on learning the principles of light transport, before adding scene-complexity:

  • •

    In stage 1, we decimate the generated scenes to $1$ k primitives and render the scene at $256\times 256$ resolution. To prioritize learning accurate coarse-scale transport, we employ full-attention at this stage. Furthermore, we gradually increase the complexity of the scene by first training exclusively on homogeneous materials ( $1$ day on $32\times$ A100 GPUs). Next we include SVBRDFs ( $1$ additional day), followed by the inclusion of environment lighting ( $1$ day; to focus training on the lighting effects, we mask out pixels that directly see the environment map), and finally adding volumetric objects ( $1$ day).

  • •

    In stage 2 we increase the primitive budget to $4$ k as well as the resolution to $512\times 512$ , and continue to train for $2$ days on the same setup.

  • •

    In stage 3, we keep the scene parameters the same, but switch from full-attention to our combined attention sink and windowed attention ( $3$ days).

  • •

    In stage 4, we increase the primitive budget to $16$ k ( $1$ week).

  • •

    Finally, in stage 5 we increase the primitive budget to $64$ k as well as the resolution to $2048\times 2048$ for another $3$ days of training.

    • Yielding a total training time of $19$ days on $32\times$ A100 GPUs. While the training cost is significant, we emphasize that once pretrained, no fine-tuning or training is needed for rendering a new scene.

    Capabilities

    Figures  and  demonstrate the capabilities of RenderFormer-V2 on a wide variety of scenes. demonstrates that RenderFormer-V2 can render, with full global light transport, scenes containing refractive surfaces (1st) including caustics, environment lighting (2nd), volumetric scattering (3rd), and textures (4th). demonstrates displacement mapping (1st), volumetric scattering (2nd), and complex scenes with a large number of primitives (3rd and 4th). Prior neural rendering methods either require per-scene fine-tuning and/or cannot support all of these effects. Compared to path tracing, RenderFormer-V2 does not require specialized code to handle displacement mapping or volumetric scattering, and it can learn such effects solely by example.15Figure 1Figure 5

    RenderFormer-V2 employs a flexible material appearance latent space for assigning material properties to surface in the scene. demonstrates that, even though our latent space is trained on materials modeled with the Disney principled BRDF model , it can also model materials not part of the training set (e.g., in this case selected measured materials from the RGL BRDF dataset ). Moreover, as our latent space is based on encoding rendered images, it can easily be retrained to encompass material appearances currently not covered (e.g., anisotropic and color changing materials).Figure 4[]5[]8

    Comparison to RenderFormer

    RenderFormer-V2 is closely related to RenderFormer ; both use a similar two-stage transformer-based pipeline. Compared to RenderFormer, RenderFormer-V2 achieves better accuracy when rendering scenes with a large number of triangles thanks to its sparse attention mechanism (). qualitatively compares render quality for a scene with varying number of triangles; the darkening at $83.2$ k triangles when rendered with RenderFormer is a direct consequence of loss of attention. We used the publicly available version of RenderFormer which is trained on $4k$ triangles; we found that training RenderFormer for larger triangle meshes is unstable. Moreover, RenderFormer-V2 is also considerably more efficient as shown in  and  thanks to the render-informed sparse attention in the view-independent stage and the SWIN-attention in the view-dependent stage respectively (all timings are measured on a single NVIDIA A100). Empirically, we found that rendering time is approximately equally distributed over both stages (i.e., view-dependent vs. view-independent). For reference, we also include timings of Blender Cycles on the same scenes using $4096$ adaptive samples per pixel (i.e., the same setting as used for the training images).[]43Figure 6Figure 9Figure 7Figure 8

    RenderFormer-V2 not only supports larger triangle meshes, it can also be more easily fine-tuned for higher image resolution. compares two scenes rendered at $512\times 512$ and $2048\times 2048$ . An interesting observation is that despite both scenes containing the same number of triangles, that at higher resolution RenderFormer-V2 is able to more faithfully render fine detailed geometry (e.g., the dragon’s claws and Lucy’s face and hand).Figure 10

    Ablation

    We ablate the different components of RenderFormer-V2’s sparse attention mechanism. shows average PSNR, SSIM , LPIPS , and HDR-FLIP  over randomly generated scenes (using the same distribution as the training data, but with a different set of environment maps, SVBRDFs, and shapes than used for training) for different ablation variants: without sliding windowed attention, without attention sink, and leaving out lighting and/or summarization token from the attention sink – each ablation variant is trained up to stage 4 ( $16$ k primitives). Only when all components are included, we achieve the highest accuracy in rendering. Surprisingly, our sparse attention outperforms full-attention, which we attribute to the full-attention model having to distribute its attention over too many tokens (i.e., loss of focus). further qualitatively demonstrates the difference in quality between the different ablation variants.     Limitations

    While RenderFormer-V2 addresses many shortcomings of RenderFormer, it is not without limitations. First, RenderFormer-V2 is still limited to maximum $8$ light sources per scene, a constraint inherited from its training data. However, we argue that more complex lighting conditions are more efficiently modeled with the addition of an environment map. Furthermore, similar to RenderFormer, our model is trained on single frames, and it does not explicitely enforce temporal coherence. While RenderFormer-V2 supports textures/SVBRDFs, the resolution is fixed per triangle primitive ( $32\times 32$ ). Consequently, significant texture-quality degradation can occur for large triangles. However, this can easily be resolved by subdividing triangles to impose a maximum triangle size. By supporting heterogeneous primitives and using a material appearance parameterization independent of a hard-coded BRDF model, RenderFormer-V2 can easily be extended to support new primitives. However, training is most effective when new primitives are added in the first training stage. Consequently, adding a new primitive typically requires significant retraining. Improving extensibility without requiring a full retraining is an interesting avenue for future research.

    9

    In this paper we presented RenderFormer-V2, a transformer-based neural rendering model that takes as input a sequence of primitives (i.e., textured triangles, volumetric elements, light sources, environment maps, and camera) and outputs a rendered image of the scene with full global illumination. RenderFormer-V2 employs a rendering-aware sparse-attention to resolve intra-primitive light transport which enables RenderFormer-V2 to scale better to larger scenes, both for training as well as inference. Furthermore, we employ a flexible latent material appearance space to specify surface reflectance. RenderFormer-V2 is trained end-to-end, thereby avoiding the need for specialized code to handle displacement mapping or volumetric scattering.

    • Appendix 0.C

    RenderFormer-V2 shares some architectural similarities with RenderFormer . To better assess the differences and improvements, we perform an in-depth comparison.[]43

    0.C.1

    contrasts the RenderFormer architecture with RenderFormer-V2’s architecture. The key differences are:Figure 3

  • 1.

    . RenderFormer encodes all primitives (including light sources) in a homogeneous triangle token. RenderFormer-V2 supports heterogeneous tokens, each with its own encoding procedure, supporting a wide range of primitives ranging from triangles, volume elements, and environment maps. In addition, RenderFormer-V2 adds support for spatially varying materials (with displacement mapping) and uses a BRDF-model-agnostic material specification.Input Tokens

  • 2.

    . Whereas RenderFormer utilizes a full (dense) self-attention, RenderFormer-V2 uses a sliding windowed attention combined with attention sinks. The sinks have rendering-aware semantics and include: global registers, light sources, and summarization tokens to model long-range light transport.View-independent Attention

  • 3.

    . RenderFormer uses full self-attention between all ray-bundle tokens. This is costly and it is unlikely that pixels far away in the image will be meaningfully related to nearby pixels. Therefore, RenderFormer-V2 uses SWIN attention instead.View-dependent Attention

    • By extending the supported token types and by adopting a novel sparse attention architecture, RenderFormer-V2 enables more accurate rendering of more complex scenes with richer visual effects.

item.title: LaTeX renderer
item.description:
来源：Simon Willison（English） 相关度：16.7 正文：2397 字 / 2 图

分类：latex / paul-ford tools urls

命中：renderer

Tool: LaTeX renderer Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the UR

15th October 2026

ToolLaTeX renderer— LaTeX renderer turns LaTeX source into a rendered view, either a single display equation typeset by MathJax or a full document or prose fragment typeset by faster-latex, with a live preview beside the editor and a toolbar switch between Edit and Rendered views. Source can be typed, loaded from a URL or GitHub Gist, or picked from built-in examples, and the page keeps the LaTeX in the URL fragment so it can be shared as a readable or compressed link.

Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner).Tiny Little Office

Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link.

#fragment

It also has telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude to generate that explains how the URL format works:an llms.txt fileused that filethis link to a deck

Tiny Little Office inspired me (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used:to have Claude Code

I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too.

Since it was working in I told it to take inspiration from the mechanism used by my existing as protection against XSS risks:my tools repo

<iframe sandbox="...">
SVG in Markdown tool

Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project

I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well:

We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool

Here's . The tool uses , , , and .an example linkPako 2.1.0MathJax 4.1.3faster-latex 0.3.1DOMPurify 3.4.16

item.title: X-Splat: Unified Gaussian Splatting for Joint RGB and X-ray 3D Reconstruction
item.description:
来源：arXiv·cs.GR 最新（English） 相关度：16.6 正文：87255 字 / 13 图

作者：Wangze Xu、Chu Zhou、Mae Yamaguchi 等 7 人

分类：cs.CV / cs.GR

接收/备注：SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers. 19 pages (12 main paper + 7 supplementary), 13 figures. Project page: https://zezeaaa.github.io/X-Splat/ ｜ DOI 10.1145/3829340.3842177

PDF：https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23237v1

命中：gaussian splatting、gaussian、splatting、rendering

Jointly reconstructing RGB and X-ray provides new insights by connecting external appearance with internal structure, enabling a more complete understanding of real-world objects than single modality. Yet existing methods train separate models per modality and suffer from redundant geometry, alignment artifacts, and loose coupling that limits cross-modal insight discovery. We propose a unified rep

License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.23237v1 [cs.CV] 16 Oct 2026

X-Splat: Unified Gaussian Splatting for Joint RGB and X-ray 3D Reconstruction

SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers; December 01–04, 2026; Kuala Lumpur, MalaysiaConference: SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers (SA Conference Papers ’26), December 01–04, 2026, Kuala Lumpur, MalaysiaDOI: 10.1145/3829340.3842177979-8-4007-2842-6/2026/12ISBN: Computing methodologies Point-based modelsCCS: Computing methodologies ReconstructionCCS: Wangze Xu , Affiliation: The University of TokyoJapanemail: xwz@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp, Chu Zhou , Affiliation: National Institute of InformaticsJapanemail: zhou_chu@pku.edu.cn, Mae Yamaguchi , Affiliation: The University of TokyoJapan, Linrui Dai , Affiliation: The University of TokyoJapan, I-Chao Shen , Affiliation: The University of TokyoJapan, Takashi Ijiri , Affiliation: Shibaura Institute of TechnologyJapan and Imari Sato , Affiliation: National Institute of InformaticsJapan, Affiliation: The University of TokyoJapanemail: imarik@nii.ac.jp© cc

Abstract.

Jointly reconstructing RGB and X-ray provides new insights by connecting external appearance with internal structure, enabling a more complete understanding of real-world objects than single modality. Yet existing methods train separate models per modality and suffer from redundant geometry, alignment artifacts, and loose coupling that limits cross-modal insight discovery. We propose a unified representation in which all Gaussian primitives share a single set of geometric parameters, with only surface-proximal primitives additionally carrying appearance attributes. We perform cross-modal registration through clean multi-view stereo and X-ray geometric proxies instead of aligning two sets of optimized Gaussians, improving alignment stability. We then jointly optimize the unified representation via supervision from both modalities, complemented by a surface-depth consistency loss derived from X-ray geometry to guide RGB reconstruction. Experiments on the InsideOut dataset and our dataset show that our framework achieves more robust cross-modal alignment, higher RGB rendering quality without compromising X-ray reconstruction, and a more compact representation than maintaining two independent geometries. Project page: .Flower & Insecthttps://zezeaaa.github.io/X-Splat/

3D Gaussian splatting, cross-modal 3D reconstruction, X-ray tomography, novel view synthesis

Keywords:

†by†cc-license:

1.

Real-world objects are both surface and interior: we readily see a flower’s outer petals, but not the structure within. Yet existing 3D reconstruction typically captures only one of the two at a time. RGB cameras record the external appearance through surface reflection, while X-ray imaging penetrates objects to reveal their internal volumetric structure through attenuation, leaving the two as separate digital records of the same physical object. We pursue a unified 3D representation that natively captures both, enabling consistent rendering of an object’s exterior and interior from any viewpoint (Fig. ). Such a unified representation supports applications such as digital cultural heritage , industrial inspection , and physically-grounded visualization , providing a more complete understanding of real objects than either modality alone.1()Bossema et al., 2024()Bergmann et al., 2019()Ni et al., 2024

Existing 3D reconstruction work has developed each modality along a separate track. RGB-based approaches built on neural radiance fields (NeRF)  and Gaussian splatting  reconstruct external surfaces but treat the object interior as unobserved space. X-ray-based methods such as NAF , X-Gaussian , and R-Gaussian  recover internal density distributions but provide no surface appearance. Training separate models per modality is a natural starting point, yet such a decoupled approach keeps two independent representations of the same object with no cross-modal alignment, increasing parameter count and preventing consistent rendering of external appearance and internal structure.()Mildenhall et al., 2021()Kerbl et al., 2023()Zha et al., 2022()Cai et al., 2024a2()Zha et al., 2024

A more principled direction is to design a single framework targeting RGB and X-ray jointly, and the recent InsideOut  is the first such attempt. It trains a separate Gaussian set per modality and bridges them through hierarchical alignment between the two optimized representations. While this design takes a first step toward joint reconstruction, it leaves several aspects underexplored. First, the two Gaussian sets independently model the same underlying geometry, doubling the parameter footprint. Second, the alignment operates on optimized Gaussian primitives that are the outcome of geometric and appearance fitting rather than a faithful description of the object’s surface, and contain floaters and optimization artifacts, leading to surface-to-interior misalignment that compromises applications requiring aligned internal-external display, such as digital cultural heritage . Finally, although the scene geometry is accurately recovered from X-ray, it is still underutilized in RGB optimization, leaving RGB weakly supervised and limiting surface fidelity in applications such as industrial inspection .()Lee et al., 2025()Bossema et al., 2024()Bergmann et al., 2019

To address these limitations, we present , a unified Gaussian framework for joint RGB-X-ray 3D reconstruction. Our design is based on a simple observation: although RGB images arise from surface reflection and X-ray images from volumetric attenuation, both are ultimately conditioned on the geometry of the same physical object. This shared geometric origin suggests that the cleanest design is not to model each modality with its own independent geometry, but to let the two modalities share a single geometric representation while specializing only the attributes that genuinely differ between them. Concretely, we propose a unified Gaussian representation in which all primitives share a single set of geometric parameters, and only primitives close to the surface carry appearance attributes, reflecting the physical fact that RGB observations arise primarily from surface reflection. This eliminates the redundancy of maintaining two independent geometries and lets gradients from both modalities flow into the same shared geometry. To bring the two modalities into a common coordinate frame, we register them through clean geometric proxies derived directly from the input data, namely a multi-view stereo (MVS)  point cloud from the RGB views and a mesh extracted from the X-ray reconstruction, rather than aligning the already-optimized Gaussians. Finally, we exploit the shared geometry to enable joint optimization across both modalities, complemented by a surface-depth consistency loss using X-ray-derived surface geometry to supervise RGB rendering. In summary, our contributions are:X-Splat(; ; ; ; )Yao et al., 2018Gu et al., 2020Yang et al., 2020Peng et al., 2022Cao et al., 2022

  • •

    with shared geometric parameters and surface-restricted appearance attributes, enabling compact joint modeling of external appearance and internal volumetric structure.A unified Gaussian representation

  • •

    using clean MVS and X-ray proxies to register two modalities, avoiding the surface-to-interior misalignment that arises when registering two sets of already-optimized Gaussians.A geometry-based alignment pipeline

  • •

    where both modalities update shared parameters via their respective objectives, complemented by an X-ray-derived surface-depth consistency loss.A joint optimization scheme

    • We evaluate on the InsideOut dataset  and a new dataset combining existing flower scans  with newly captured insect specimens, broadening evaluation to natural objects. Our method achieves more robust cross-modal alignment, better RGB rendering quality without compromising X-ray reconstruction, and is more compact than two independent models.X-Splat()Lee et al., 2025Flower & Insect()Ijiri et al., 2014

    2.

    External Appearance Reconstruction

    Neural radiance fields (NeRF) have substantially advanced the appearance reconstruction of 3D objects from RGB images, which established a differentiable volume-rendering paradigm that fits a continuous radiance field to multi-view images. Subsequent work improved its rendering quality and efficiency through multi-scale anti-aliasing  and hash-grid encodings . A parallel line replaces the volumetric formulation with neural implicit surfaces  to recover sharper geometry. More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting  represents the scene with explicit Gaussian primitives and a tile-based rasterizer, achieving real-time rendering at comparable visual quality, with Mip-Splatting  addressing aliasing under varying sampling rates. Subsequent work has improved surface fidelity by reformulating the primitives as 2D disks  or regularizing them toward the underlying surface . Other lines extend to sparse-view , pose-free , and dynamic  settings. While these methods achieve high-quality external appearance reconstruction, the internal structure of objects remains beyond their scope.()Mildenhall et al., 2021()Barron et al., 2021()Müller et al., 2022(; )Wang et al., 2021Yariv et al., 2021()Kerbl et al., 2023()Yu et al., 2024()Huang et al., 2024()Guédon and Lepetit, 2024(; ; ; ; ; )Deng et al., 2022Wang et al., 2023Li et al., 2024bZhu et al., 2024Xu et al., 2024Peng et al., 2024(; ; ; ; )Fan et al., 2024Fu et al., 2024Shen et al., 2024Ye et al., 2025Wang et al., 2025(; ; ; ; ; ; )Fridovich-Keil et al., 2023Yang et al., 2024Wu et al., 2024Qian et al., 2024Hu et al., 2024Xu et al., 2025Zhan et al., 2025

    Internal Structure Reconstruction

    X-ray and computed tomography (CT) reconstruction  recovers the internal density distribution of an object from projection measurements. Classical analytical methods such as FDK  remain the standard for cone-beam CT, producing volumetric reconstructions in closed form when projections are dense. To handle sparse-view settings, NAF  adapts a neural attenuation field to fit projection measurements with a continuous network representation, and SAX-NeRF  employs a line-segment Transformer to capture spatial structure from X-ray projections. More recently, Gaussian splatting has been extended to the X-ray modality. X-Gaussian  replaces alpha-compositing with a radiative rasterizer that follows the Beer-Lambert law, enabling efficient X-ray novel-view synthesis. R-Gaussian  further corrects an integration bias in this rasterization formulation and introduces a differentiable voxelizer that enables accurate tomographic reconstruction. Subsequent work also explores direction-disentangled volume rendering for realistic radiographs . While these methods achieve high-quality internal density reconstruction, external surface appearance lies beyond the X-ray modality.(; ; )Gordon et al., 1970Li et al., 2023Yu et al., 2025()Feldkamp et al., 1984()Zha et al., 2022()Cai et al., 2024b()Cai et al., 2024a2()Zha et al., 2024()Gao et al., 2024

    Cross-modal 3D Reconstruction

    3D reconstruction has long benefited from auxiliary modalities captured by physical sensors that complement RGB cameras. Depth sensors such as LiDAR and commodity time-of-flight devices provide direct geometric measurements that supplement photometric supervision in driving  and indoor scenes . Thermal and infrared imaging extend RGB reconstruction to scenarios invisible to RGB cameras, with recent work introducing implicit neural fusion of far-infrared and RGB imagery . Multi-spectral and hyperspectral cameras likewise enrich RGB reconstruction with material- and wavelength-specific signals . Recent Gaussian-splatting frameworks further model RGB jointly with thermal images , or with multiple modalities through shared and modality-specific Gaussian components . These auxiliary modalities all carry surface-domain signals, leaving the reconstructed target on the externally observable surface. Few works have attempted to combine external appearance with internal structure. Joining RGB and X-ray for 3D reconstruction differs fundamentally, since they arise from different physical mechanisms. Prior combinations of the two modalities operate at the image level in medical image fusion  or serve geometric calibration between the two sensing systems , and learned priors have been used to predict unseen object thickness from RGB-D observations . None of these produces a unified 3D representation of appearance and internal structure. The most relevant prior work is InsideOut , which hierarchically fits two independently optimized Gaussian sets and bridges them by a post-hoc visual alignment. In contrast, we align via purely geometric registration and adopt a unified representation with shared geometric parameters, enabling truly joint optimization.(; )Rematas et al., 2022Sun et al., 2024()Keetha et al., 2024(; )Li et al., 2024aHassan et al., 2024(; )Thirgood et al., 2025Meyer et al., 2025()Lu et al., 2025()Gu and Wang, 2025()Nair and Singh, 2018()Albiol et al., 2016()Nicastro et al., 2019()Lee et al., 2025

    3.

    Imaging Formation: Reflection vs. Transmission

    RGB and X-ray imaging differ fundamentally in how light interacts with matter. In RGB imaging, most of the radiance received along a camera ray originates near the first surface it encounters on an opaque object, and the observed pixel intensity is modeled as the integral of emitted color along the ray, weighted by accumulated transmittance,

    (1) $I_{\mathrm{rgb}}(\mathbf{r})=\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{f}}T(t)\,\alpha\bigl(\mathbf{r}(t)\bigr)\,c\bigl(\mathbf{r}(t)\bigr)\,dt,\>T(t)=\exp\!\left(-\int_{t_{n}}^{t}\alpha\bigl(\mathbf{r}(s)\bigr)\,ds\right),$

    where $\alpha(\cdot)$ and $c(\cdot)$ are the volumetric opacity and color fields, $t_{n}$ and $t_{f}$ are the near and far bounds of the ray, and $T(t)$ is the transmittance from the camera to depth $t$ . In contrast, an X-ray penetrates the object along its entire path, and the log-domain pixel value is the line integral of the density field $\sigma(\cdot)$ along the ray, governed by the Beer–Lambert law,

    (2) $I_{\mathrm{xray}}(\mathbf{r})=\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{f}}\sigma\bigl(\mathbf{r}(t)\bigr)\,dt.$

    Despite these distinct optical mechanisms, both modalities observe the same underlying object, and each is a different forward operator acting on a common 3D geometry.

    3D Gaussian Representation

    3D Gaussian splatting  models a scene as $N$ anisotropic 3D Gaussians, each with a center $\mu_{i}$ and a covariance $\Sigma_{i}=R_{i}S_{i}S_{i}^{\top}R_{i}^{\top}$ decomposed into a rotation $R_{i}$ and a diagonal scale $S_{i}$ . RGB and X-ray Gaussian splatting share these geometry parameters $\{\mu_{i},R_{i},S_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ and differ in their per-primitive optical attributes and rendering operator.()Kerbl et al., 2023

    Each primitive additionally carries an opacity $\alpha_{i}\in[0,1]$ and a view-dependent color $c_{i}$ encoded by spherical harmonics . Primitives are projected onto the image plane by EWA splatting , and the pixel color is obtained by depth-ordered front-to-back compositing of the projected 2D footprints,RGB Gaussian Splatting.()Kerbl et al., 2023()Zwicker et al., 2001

    (3) $I_{\mathrm{rgb}}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{r})}c_{i}\,\alpha^{\prime}_{i}\prod_{j

    where $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{r})$ is the depth-ordered set of primitives intersected by ray  $\mathbf{r}$ and $\alpha^{\prime}_{i}$ is the EWA-projected effective opacity.

    Each primitive instead carries a single scalar density $\rho_{i}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}$ , since X-ray attenuation depends only on isotropic material density. Integrating the resulting density field along the ray according to Eq. () yields, in closed form, a sum of 2D Gaussians on the detector ,Radiative Gaussian Splatting.2(; )Cai et al., 2024aZha et al., 2024

    (4) $I_{\mathrm{xray}}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat{\rho}_{i}\;\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{2D}}\!\bigl(\hat{\mathbf{x}};\,\hat{\mu}_{i},\,\hat{\Sigma}_{i}\bigr),$

    where $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ , $\hat{\mu}_{i}$ , $\hat{\Sigma}_{i}$ , and $\hat{\rho}_{i}$ are obtained by projective mapping .     4.

    Given calibrated RGB views $\{I^{\mathrm{rgb}}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K_{C}}$ and X-ray projections $\{I^{\mathrm{xray}}_{l}\}_{l=1}^{K_{X}}$ of the same physical object, our goal is to recover a single unified Gaussian set $\{\mathcal{G}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ that jointly supports high-fidelity RGB novel-view rendering and X-ray novel-projection rendering. As illustrated in Fig. , a coarse X-ray reconstruction first anchors cross-modal alignment (Sec. ) and initializes the unified Gaussian set, in which appearance attributes are restricted to a surface subset for compactness (Sec. ); the unified set is then jointly optimized under both modalities, bridged by a surface-aware initialization (Secs. –).24.24.14.34.4

    4.1.

    We represent the object by a single set of $N$ Gaussian primitives $\{\mathcal{G}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ . Each primitive $\mathcal{G}_{i}$ carries shared geometry parameters $\{\mu_{i},R_{i},S_{i}\}$ , a radiative attribute given by a density $\rho_{i}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}$ , and, for primitives in a surface subset $\mathcal{S}\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$ , additional appearance attributes consisting of an opacity $\alpha_{i}$ and a view-dependent color $c_{i}$ . The shared geometry parameters follow the parametrization in Sec.  and are used by both renderers, while the radiative and appearance attributes are specific to X-ray and RGB rendering respectively. We write a primitive compactly as3

    (5) $\mathcal{G}_{i}=\bigl\{\underbrace{\mu_{i},R_{i},S_{i}}_{\text{shared geometry}},\;\underbrace{\rho_{i}}_{\text{radiative attribute}},\;\underbrace{\{\alpha_{i},c_{i}\}\text{ if }i\in\mathcal{S}}_{\text{appearance attributes}}\bigr\}.$

    This restriction has a physical motivation. Restricting appearance attributes to $\mathcal{S}$ reflects the physics of the two modalities. For the opaque objects considered in this work, surface reflection dominates the RGB signal, and interior primitives contribute negligibly to any RGB pixel. Note that only the geometric parameters are shared across modalities; the optical attributes $\rho$ and $\{\alpha,c\}$ remain modality-specific. The construction of $\mathcal{S}$ is detailed in Sec. .4.3

    Sharing the geometry parameters $\{\mu_{i},R_{i},S_{i}\}$ across both modalities, rather than maintaining a separate Gaussian set per modality, is motivated by three considerations. , RGB reflection and X-ray transmission are different forward operators acting on the same underlying object (Sec. ), so a single shared geometry is more faithful than aligning two independently reconstructed geometries post-hoc. , the shared design allocates $\{\mu,R,S\}$ only once and $\{\alpha,c\}$ only for $i\in\mathcal{S}$ , yielding a substantially smaller parameter count than two separate single-modality reconstructions. , gradients from both modalities update the shared geometry, anchoring it under X-ray supervision and compensating for the indirect geometric signal of RGB photometry alone.Physically3Compactness-wiseOptimization-wise

    4.2.

    Joint optimization of the unified representation requires the RGB and X-ray modalities to reside in a common coordinate frame. We therefore seek a similarity transformation $T\in\textsc{Sim}(3)$ that maps RGB camera poses into the X-ray coordinate frame. Unlike aligning two sets of optimized Gaussian primitives directly , which are corrupted by floaters and optimization artifacts, we align on clean geometric proxies extracted from each modality (Fig. ).()Lee et al., 20253

    For the RGB side, we run MVSFormer  on the calibrated RGB views and their camera parameters $\{I^{\mathrm{rgb}}_{k},\pi^{\mathrm{rgb}}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K_{C}}$ to obtain an external surface point cloud $\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{mvs}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathrm{mvs}}\times 3}$ . For the X-ray side, we first run a coarse X-ray-only optimization (Sec. ) to obtain a coarse Gaussian set $\mathcal{G}^{\mathrm{coarse}}$ , voxelize it via the differentiable voxelizer of R-Gaussian  into a CT volume, isolate the outer shell by binarization and morphological closing, extract the CT mesh via Marching Cubes , and uniformly sample its surface to obtain the point cloud $\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{ct}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathrm{ct}}\times 3}$ .()Cao et al., 20224.32()Zha et al., 2024()Lorensen and Cline, 1998

    With these two surface point clouds, we estimate the transformation $T$ by registering $\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{mvs}}$ against $\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{ct}}$ in two steps. We first perform principal component analysis (PCA) on each point cloud’s positions and align the resulting centroids, principal axes, and variances to obtain an initial similarity transformation $T^{\mathrm{pca}}$ matching translation, rotation, and scale. Starting from $T^{\mathrm{pca}}$ , we then apply point-to-point iterative closest point (ICP)  with scaling to obtain the final transformation $T$ . We apply $T$ to all RGB camera poses in homogeneous form,(; )Besl and McKay, 1992Rusinkiewicz and Levoy, 2001

    (6) $E^{\mathrm{rgb}\to\mathrm{ct}}_{k}=E^{\mathrm{rgb}}_{k}\,T^{-1},$

    where $E^{\mathrm{rgb}}_{k}$ is the world-to-camera extrinsic of the $k$ -th RGB view.

    4.3.

    The two modalities provide complementary supervision, but X-ray imposes stronger constraints on the shared geometry than RGB. We exploit this asymmetry by establishing the shared geometry from X-ray first, then refining appearance attributes against this anchor.

    A coarse X-ray-only optimization suffices to recover a reliable shared geometry that benefits both the alignment in Sec.  and the subsequent RGB learning. We therefore split the optimization into two stages. In Stage 1, only the X-ray-related parameters $\{\mu_{i},R_{i},S_{i},\rho_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ are optimized under the X-ray photometric loss alone, starting from a standard FDK reconstruction . This produces the coarse X-ray Gaussian set $\mathcal{G}^{\mathrm{coarse}}$ used in Sec.  for CT mesh extraction. In Stage 2, the appearance attributes $\{\alpha_{i},c_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{S}}$ are allocated and initialized as described below, the X-ray-related parameters $\{\mu_{i},R_{i},S_{i},\rho_{i}\}$ are inherited from their Stage 1 values, and all parameters are optimized jointly. We retain the X-ray photometric loss throughout Stage 2 rather than freezing the X-ray side, since RGB gradients could otherwise drift the shared geometry to improve appearance at the cost of X-ray fidelity.Staged schedule.4.2(; )Feldkamp et al., 1984Zha et al., 20244.2

    The surface subset $\mathcal{S}$ introduced in Eq. () partitions the primitives into surface primitives, which carry both the radiative and appearance attributes, and interior primitives, which carry only the shared geometry parameters and the radiative attribute. This partition selectively allocates appearance attributes on top of a shared backbone, rather than splitting the primitives into RGB-only and X-ray-only sets. We construct $\mathcal{S}$ from the CT mesh extracted during alignment to fully leverage the X-ray surface geometry as a prior for RGB optimization, and also to keep the representation compact by preventing interior primitives from participating in RGB rendering. Let $d_{i}$ denote the distance from $\mu_{i}$ to the CT mesh. The surface set is defined by thresholding,Surface-aware initialization.5

    (7) $\mathcal{S}=\{\,i:d_{i}<\tau_{d}\,\},$

    where $\tau_{d}$ is a distance threshold in the CT coordinate frame. For $i\in\mathcal{S}$ , the opacity is initialized as a Gaussian decay,

    (8) $\alpha_{i}=\alpha_{\mathrm{surf}}\cdot\exp\!\left(-\frac{d_{i}^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right),$

    with $\alpha_{\mathrm{surf}}$ a reference opacity and $\sigma$ a decay scale proportional to $\tau_{d}$ , so that primitives lying directly on the surface receive the largest initial opacity. The color $c_{i}$ is initialized from the color of the nearest point in $\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{mvs}}$ . The membership of $\mathcal{S}$ is updated throughout training, with details deferred to Sec. .4.4

    The unified representation enables us to render an RGB surface depth $D^{\mathrm{rgb}}$ and a CT reference depth $D^{\mathrm{ct}}$ from a common viewpoint. $D^{\mathrm{rgb}}$ reuses Eq. () with the along-ray depth $z_{i}$ in place of $c_{i}$ , restricted to $i\in\mathcal{S}$ ; $D^{\mathrm{ct}}$ is rasterized from the X-ray mesh, which is periodically re-extracted from the evolving X-ray volume during Stage 2. To exploit the X-ray geometric signal beyond the photometric term without forcing pixel-wise depth agreement, we apply an edge-aware smoothness loss in which the CT depth supplies only edge structure as a stop-gradient target,X-ray-derived geometric constraints.3

    (9) $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{r}}\!\left[\frac{1}{\bar{D}^{\mathrm{ct}}}\sum_{a\in\{x,y\}}\exp\!\bigl(-|\nabla_{a}D^{\mathrm{ct}}|/\tau\bigr)\,|\nabla_{a}D^{\mathrm{rgb}}|\right],$

    where $\nabla_{a}$ is the spatial depth gradient along image axis $a$ and $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{r}}$ averages over valid foreground pixels, with $\tau$ set to the median of in-mask CT gradient magnitudes and $\bar{D}^{\mathrm{ct}}$ the mean foreground CT depth as a scale normalizer. The loss permits RGB depth discontinuities only where the CT depth has edges, aligning the surface boundary structure of the two depth maps without constraining absolute depth values.

    The Stage 1 objective combines the L1 plus D-SSIM X-ray photometric loss $\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{xray}}_{\mathrm{photo}}$ with the 3D total-variation regularizer $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TV}}$ of R-Gaussian ,Overall objective.2()Zha et al., 2024

    (10) $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{stage1}}=\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{xray}}_{\mathrm{photo}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{tv}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TV}}.$

    The Stage 2 objective adds an L1 plus D-SSIM RGB photometric loss $\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{rgb}}_{\mathrm{photo}}$ and the geometric consistency loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}}$ ,

    (11) $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{stage2}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{rgb}}\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{rgb}}_{\mathrm{photo}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{xray}}\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{xray}}_{\mathrm{photo}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{tv}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TV}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{geo}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}},$

    4.4.

    We extend the adaptive density control of 3DGS  to the unified setting. We maintain two independent position-gradient statistics per primitive, $\bar{g}^{\mathrm{rgb}}_{i}$ and $\bar{g}^{\mathrm{xray}}_{i}$ , computed separately for each modality since the two modalities differ in backward frequency and loss scale. In Stage 2, the set of primitives selected for cloning or splitting is()Kerbl et al., 2023

    (12) $\mathcal{D}=\bigl\{\,\mathcal{G}_{i}\;\big|\;i\in\{1,\ldots,N\},\;\;\bar{g}^{\mathrm{xray}}_{i}\geq\theta^{\mathrm{xray}}\;\lor\;(\bar{g}^{\mathrm{rgb}}_{i}\geq\theta^{\mathrm{rgb}}\;\land\;i\in\mathcal{S})\,\bigr\},$

    so that under-fitting in either modality drives the addition of new primitives, where $\theta^{\mathrm{xray}}$ and $\theta^{\mathrm{rgb}}$ are the per-modality gradient densification thresholds. The RGB branch is further restricted to $\mathcal{S}$ since interior primitives carry no appearance attributes; the X-ray branch is unrestricted because X-ray supervision legitimately requires primitives throughout the object interior. New primitives inherit the surface-set membership of their parent. For pruning, removing primitives based on low opacity alone is too aggressive, since a primitive may be invisible to RGB rendering yet carry meaningful X-ray density. We instead require both attributes to be low:

    (13) $\mathcal{R}=\bigl\{\,\mathcal{G}_{i}\;\big|\;i\in\{1,\ldots,N\},\;\;\alpha_{i}<\alpha_{\min}\;\land\;\rho_{i}<\rho_{\min}\,\bigr\}.$

    where $\alpha_{\min}$ and $\rho_{\min}$ are the minimum opacity and density thresholds. At each densification interval, primitives in $\mathcal{S}$ whose opacity has fallen below $\alpha_{\min}$ are demoted out of $\mathcal{S}$ rather than pruned, so they no longer participate in RGB rendering but continue contributing to X-ray rendering. In Stage 1, only the X-ray-related criteria apply since no appearance attributes exist yet. The full training procedure is detailed in the supplementary material.

    5.

    5.1.

    Datasets.

    We evaluate our method on two datasets covering nine scenes. The first is the InsideOut dataset , which provides four scenes (Matryoshka, Pharaoh, Skull, and Toy Gun) with paired RGB photographs and ground-truth CT volumes. The second, which we refer to as the dataset, contains two flower scenes (Tulip, Eustoma) from  and three insect scenes (E02, E15, E32) acquired from prepared specimens, all with paired CT volumes. To evaluate all baselines under identical X-ray acquisition geometry, we follow the protocol of R-Gaussian  and re-synthesize cone-beam projections from ground-truth CT volume using TIGRE , sampling 50 training and 120 testing projections uniformly over $[0^{\circ},360^{\circ})$ at $512\times 512$ resolution. For RGB, we use the real photographs released by InsideOut , the Blender-rendered views of the real-specimen Flower assets , and our captured photographs of the prepared insect specimens, all downsampled to width $800$ . We hold out every fourth view for testing and train on the remainder. More details are in the supplementary material.()Lee et al., 2025Flower & Insect()Ijiri et al., 20142()Zha et al., 2024()Biguri et al., 2016()Lee et al., 2025()Ijiri et al., 2014

    Metrics.

    For RGB, we report PSNR, SSIM , and LPIPS  on held-out test views inside per-view foreground masks. For X-ray, we follow R-Gaussian  and report 2D-PSNR/SSIM on rendered projections and 3D-PSNR between the reconstructed and ground-truth CT volumes. For the alignment, we report Chamfer Distance (CD) between the aligned MVS and X-ray surfaces as a direct measure of cross-modal alignment, in normalized scene units where each object’s longest extent equals  $2$ . For compactness, we report the number of Gaussians (#G (k) in thousands) and storage (MB).()Wang et al., 2004()Zhang et al., 20182()Zha et al., 2024

    Implementation Details.

    We implement our framework on top of the R-Gaussian  codebase and reuse its X-ray training schedule for Stage 1. Stage 1 runs for $3{,}000$ iterations from an FDK initialization , optimizing $\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{xray}}_{\mathrm{photo}}$ together with the $3$ D total-variation regularizer at $\lambda_{\mathrm{tv}}=0.05$ . After Stage 1 we extract the CT mesh, recover the geometry-based alignment (Sec. ), and construct the surface set with surface distance threshold $\tau_{d}=0.02$ and reference opacity $\alpha_{\mathrm{surf}}=0.5$ . Stage 2 then jointly optimizes the unified representation for $12{,}000$ iterations under $\lambda_{\mathrm{rgb}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{xray}}=1.0$ , $\lambda_{\mathrm{tv}}=0.05$ , and $\lambda_{\mathrm{geo}}=0.05$ . Each photometric loss combines $\mathcal{L}_{1}$ with D-SSIM at $\lambda_{\mathrm{dssim}}^{\mathrm{xray}}=0.25$ and $\lambda_{\mathrm{dssim}}^{\mathrm{rgb}}=0.2$ . The CT mesh is re-extracted every $500$ iterations during Stage 2, and $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}}$ is computed on $180$ virtual cameras sampled by Fibonacci sphere. All other hyperparameters follow 3DGS defaults ; complete settings, learning rates, and densification thresholds are listed in the supplementary material. Training takes approximately $14$ – $21$ minutes per InsideOut scene on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. As the official InsideOut  implementation is not publicly available, we reproduce their method by following the descriptions and hyperparameters reported in their paper. Specifically, InsideOut’s final X-ray Gaussians come from its X-ray-only stage 2 (matching R-Gaussian); we omit its subsequent X-ray refinement because the opacity-based rendering there is incompatible with our density-based renderer. We denote this reproduction by InsideOut in all tables and figures. The full reproduction setup and a discussion of discrepancies with its originally reported results are provided in the supplementary material.2()Zha et al., 2024()Feldkamp et al., 19844.2()Kerbl et al., 2023()Lee et al., 20252†

    5.2.

    Tables  and  report per-modality novel-view metrics on both datasets, with sub-tables (a) for RGB rendering and (b) for X-ray reconstruction. On the RGB side, Ours achieves consistently competitive metrics across all scenes on both datasets, improving over either 3DGS variant by around 1 dB PSNR on InsideOut and over 2 dB on Flower & Insect. Even FDK initialization, which already encodes the full volumetric structure, fails to outperform the MVS-init baseline, confirming that better initial geometry alone cannot break the single-modality ceiling without persistent geometric supervision. InsideOut yields substantially lower RGB quality in our experiments (reproduction setup in Sec. ). On the X-ray side, our representation produces reconstruction quality consistent with R-Gaussian  across both datasets, with only minor fluctuations across individual metrics, while the classical FDK reconstruction degrades substantially compared to the Gaussian-based methods. The qualitative results shown in Fig.  and Fig.  suggest that our method recovers sharper surface texture and fewer floater artifacts than all RGB baselines on scenes such as Matryoshka and Tulip, and our reconstructed CT slices and X-ray projections produce details closely matching R-Gaussian on scenes from both datasets. Joint training over a shared geometry therefore substantially improves RGB reconstruction quality without compromising X-ray reconstruction fidelity, validating the staged optimization of Sec. .12†()Lee et al., 20255.12()Zha et al., 20244524.3

    Table  reports Chamfer Distance to the X-ray-reconstructed surface for our alignment pipeline and three representative alternatives, all applied to the same source point cloud and the same target geometry so that only the estimated similarity transformation $T$ varies. As shown by both Table  and Fig.  (e.g., the residual misalignment on Skull), the InsideOut hierarchical alignment is less accurate than the other three methods. It operates on optimized Gaussian primitives whose floaters and overfit details propagate directly into the alignment. In contrast, aligning the clean MVS surface and CT mesh proxies with PCA alone already outperforms the InsideOut hierarchical alignment, and our full PCA+ICP pipeline improves Chamfer Distance by roughly $8\times$ . The geometric cleanliness of the alignment source is therefore more decisive than the alignment algorithm itself. PCA provides global orientation and scale alignment, while ICP refines the result locally. PCA alone is insufficient for fine alignment, and identity-initialized ICP without a good PCA seed can fall into local minima and even collapse to near-degenerate scales on symmetric objects (e.g., E15 in Fig. ). The two stages are therefore complementary.Cross-Modal Alignment.3377

    6.

    We presented a unified Gaussian framework for joint reconstruction of external surface appearance and internal volumetric structure. A single set of Gaussian primitives shares geometric parameters across both modalities, with appearance attributes restricted to surface-proximal primitives; cross-modal registration uses clean geometric proxies; and joint optimization is complemented by an X-ray-derived surface-depth consistency loss. Our design improves RGB rendering quality, yields more robust cross-modal alignment than post-hoc strategies, preserves X-ray fidelity, and is substantially more compact than two independent models.

    First, our appearance model assumes that surface reflection dominates the RGB signal and therefore restricts appearance attributes to surface-proximal primitives. This assumption does not hold for transparent objects such as glass, or for materials with strong subsurface scattering or transmission (e.g., biological tissue or wax), whose appearance arises from light interacting with the object interior. Supporting such materials would require a volumetric appearance model, and paired RGB–X-ray datasets containing them are not yet available; we leave this to future work. Second, our framework depends on a reasonably accurate X-ray reconstruction to anchor the shared geometry, and may degrade when the X-ray inputs are extremely noisy or blurry. Third, current joint training improves RGB but matches the single-modality baseline on X-ray; extending RGB supervision to also benefit X-ray reconstruction is left as future work.Limitations and future work.
